Vignette:
A 28-year-old woman who is 3 weeks postpartum and exclusively breastfeeding presents with a 2-day history of increasing pain, redness, and swelling in her right breast. She reports associated fever and chills and feeling generally unwell. She had been experiencing nipple soreness and cracking on the right side and notes the baby has had difficulty latching on that side. She denies palpable masses or nipple discharge other than breast milk. Vital signs show temperature 101.2°F, heart rate 94, blood pressure 118/72. On examination, there is a wedge-shaped area of erythema, warmth, and induration in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast. The area is exquisitely tender to palpation. There is no fluctuance or palpable abscess. The ipsilateral nipple shows a small fissure. Axillary lymph nodes are mildly enlarged on the right.

Vignette:
A 22-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes diagnosed at age 8 presents with 2 days of worsening nausea, vomiting, diffuse abdominal pain, and progressive lethargy. She reports that she ran out of insulin 3 days ago and could not afford a refill. On examination, she is drowsy but arousable, markedly dehydrated with dry mucous membranes and poor skin turgor. Vital signs: T 36.4C, HR 128, RR 32 (deep, labored Kussmaul respirations), BP 92/54, SpO2 99%. Her breath has a distinct fruity acetone odor. Abdomen is diffusely tender without peritoneal signs. Labs: glucose 486 mg/dL, pH 7.08, pCO2 14 mmHg, bicarbonate 4 mEq/L, anion gap 32, beta-hydroxybutyrate 8.2 mmol/L, potassium 5.6 mEq/L (expected to drop with treatment), sodium 128 mEq/L (corrected 134), BUN 38 mg/dL, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL.

Vignette:
A 58-year-old man presents with sudden onset of severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back between his shoulder blades that began 45 minutes ago while lifting heavy boxes. He has a history of poorly controlled hypertension and takes amlodipine intermittently. On examination, he is writhing in pain and appears ashen. Vital signs: T 36.8C, HR 108, RR 24, BP 210/118 in the right arm and 162/90 in the left arm. A diastolic murmur is auscultated along the left sternal border. Pulses are diminished in the left upper extremity. Chest X-ray shows widened mediastinum. CT angiography of the chest reveals a Stanford type A dissection originating in the ascending aorta with an intimal flap extending into the aortic arch.

Vignette:
A 45-yr-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 6-h history of acute-onset
left-sided lower abdominal pain. He describes the pain as starting over his left flank and
radiating down toward his groin. The pain comes and goes but is intense when present. He has
had some mild nausea without vomiting. The pain does not change with eating. The pain is less
when he walks around than when he sits or lies down flat. He has not had any bloody stools,
black stools, or change in bowel habits. He denies having diarrhea and constipation. He has
noticed his urine looks "dark" but denies pain during urination and urinary frequency. He says
that he swims several times a week for exercise, and this pain started immediately after
swimming. He also notes that several days ago, his son ran into his left side while playing
football. He took some acetaminophen, which minimally relieved his discomfort. He now
presents for evaluation at the emergency department because the pain has not subsided. He
says he has never experienced pain like this.

Vignette:
A 65-year-old man with a history of metastatic prostate cancer (Gleason 9, diagnosed 2 years ago) presents with 10 days of progressive mid-back pain and 4 days of increasing difficulty walking. He now requires a walker. He also reports a band-like sensation around his trunk at the level of the umbilicus and difficulty initiating urination. On examination, he appears cachectic. Vital signs are stable. Neurological exam reveals increased tone and spasticity in both lower extremities, bilateral lower extremity weakness (3/5 hip flexors, 4/5 knee extensors), hyperreflexia with bilateral ankle clonus, upgoing plantar responses (positive Babinski bilaterally), and a sensory level at approximately T10. MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrates a large epidural mass at T9-T10 causing significant spinal cord compression with cord signal changes.

Vignette:
A 28-year-old man presents with a persistent dry cough for the past 10 days. He reports that the cough started after a mild upper respiratory illness with sore throat and nasal congestion that has since resolved. He is a non-smoker and has no history of asthma or chronic lung disease. He denies fever, hemoptysis, or significant sputum production. On examination, vital signs are within normal limits. Lungs reveal occasional scattered rhonchi that clear with coughing. There are no wheezes or crackles. Oxygen saturation is 98% on room air.

Vignette:
A 22-year-old sexually active man presents with a 4-day history of gradually worsening left scrotal pain and swelling. The pain is dull and aching and radiates to the left inguinal region. He reports mild dysuria and a small amount of urethral discharge noticed over the past week. He has had a new sexual partner in the past month and inconsistently uses barrier protection. He denies fever, nausea, vomiting, or testicular trauma. Vital signs are normal. On examination, the left hemiscrotum is swollen and erythematous. There is tenderness and induration localized to the left epididymis posterior to the testis. Prehn sign is positive with relief of pain on elevation of the left testis. The cremasteric reflex is present bilaterally. There is no testicular torsion on clinical assessment. Urinalysis shows 15 to 20 WBC per high-power field. A nucleic acid amplification test for chlamydia and gonorrhea is sent.

Vignette:
An 18-month-old toddler presents with 1 week of rhinorrhea, cough, and congestion. Her parents report she is irritable, sleeping restlessly, and not eating well. Overnight she developed a fever. She attends day care and both parents smoke. On examination signs are found consistent with a viral respiratory infection including rhinorrhea and congestion. The toddler appears irritable and apprehensive and has a fever. Otoscopy reveals a bulging, erythematous tympanic membrane and absent landmarks.

Vignette:
A 30-year-old man presents with a painful fluid-filled blister on his right heel that developed after a 15-kilometer hike in recently purchased boots yesterday. He reports the boots felt slightly tight in the heel area. He denies any popping of the blister or signs of infection. He has no history of diabetes or peripheral neuropathy. On examination, there is a single, tense, clear fluid-filled blister approximately 2 cm in diameter on the posterior right heel. The surrounding skin is mildly erythematous. There is no purulence, surrounding warmth, streaking, or malodor. Pedal pulses are intact and sensation is normal.

Vignette:
A 42-year-old female data entry clerk presents with a 4-month history of numbness, tingling, and burning sensation in her right thumb, index finger, middle finger, and radial half of the ring finger. Symptoms are worse at night and frequently wake her from sleep. She reports shaking her hand provides temporary relief. She has also noticed progressive weakness in her grip, with difficulty holding small objects and occasional dropping of items. She works 8 hours daily at a keyboard with minimal ergonomic support. She has a history of well-controlled hypothyroidism. On examination, there is decreased sensation to two-point discrimination in the median nerve distribution. Thenar eminence shows early atrophy compared to the left. Tinel sign at the wrist is positive with paresthesias radiating to the fingers. Phalen test reproduces symptoms within 20 seconds. Grip and pinch strength are reduced on the right.

Vignette:
A 12-year-old boy is brought by his parents for a persistent cough that has lasted 3 weeks and is progressively worsening. The illness began with 1 week of runny nose and mild cough that was initially thought to be a cold. His vaccination records show he received DTaP at 2, 4, and 6 months but missed his preschool and adolescent boosters. Vital signs are normal between episodes. Lungs are clear to auscultation. A nasopharyngeal swab PCR for Bordetella pertussis returns positive. CBC shows a white blood cell count of 18,000 with 70% lymphocytes.

Vignette:
A 63-year-old man sustained a cut on his hand while gardening. His immunization history is significant for not having received a complete tetanus immunization schedule. He presents with signs of generalized tetanus with trismus ("lock jaw"), which results in a grimace described as "risus sardonicus" (sardonic smile). Intermittent tonic contraction of his skeletal muscles causes intensely painful spasms, which last for minutes, during which he retains consciousness. The spasms are triggered by external (noise, light, drafts, physical contact) or internal stimuli, and as a result he is at the risk of sustaining fractures or developing rhabdomyolysis. The tetanic spasms also produce opisthotonus, board-like abdominal wall rigidity, dysphagia, and apneic periods due to contraction of the thoracic muscles and/or glottal or pharyngeal muscles. During a generalized spasm the patient arches his back, extends his legs, flexes his arms in abduction, and clenches his fists. Apnea results during some of the spasms. Autonomic overactivity initially manifests as irritability, restlessness, sweating, and tachycardia. Several days later this may present as hyperpyrexia, cardiac arrhythmias, labile hypertension, or hypotension.

Vignette:

Vignette:
A 60-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of progressively worsening left lower quadrant abdominal pain that is constant and dull. She reports low-grade fever and mild nausea but no vomiting. CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast demonstrates sigmoid diverticulitis with pericolic fat stranding and no abscess or perforation.

Vignette:

Respirations: 16/min

Vignette:
Mrs. L is a 61 year-old woman who presents with 4 days of a cough productive of yellow sputum. Her symptoms started 4 days ago with rhinorrhea and productive cough. She initially had fevers as high as 101 for 2 days, but those have now resolved. In the office, she has normal vital signs and a normal physical examination. She is otherwise healthy except for high cholesterol for which she is being treated with atorvastatin. She has no drug allergies.

Vignette:
A 9-month-old male infant is brought in by his parents after 8 hours of episodic inconsolable crying during which he draws his legs up to his abdomen, alternating with periods of lethargy. The parents report two episodes of vomiting and one bowel movement containing dark red mucus-like material. He had a viral upper respiratory infection last week. On examination, during a pain-free interval, the infant is pale and lethargic. Vital signs: T 37.4C, HR 168, RR 36, BP 80/52. Abdomen is mildly distended with a palpable sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant. The right lower quadrant feels empty (Dance sign). Rectal exam reveals currant jelly stool on the examining finger. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates a target sign (doughnut sign) in the right upper quadrant, confirming ileocolic intussusception, with no evidence of perforation or peritonitis. Air enema reduction is arranged.

Vignette:
A 70-year-old man with a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia presents to his primary care physician with a 3-day history of dysuria, urinary frequency, and urgency. He reports mild suprapubic discomfort and low-grade fever of 100.4°F. He denies flank pain, rigors, or hematuria. His past medical history is notable for BPH managed with tamsulosin. On examination, he appears mildly uncomfortable but is in no acute distress. Vital signs show temperature 100.4°F, blood pressure 138/82, heart rate 78. Abdominal examination reveals mild suprapubic tenderness without guarding. Digital rectal exam shows an enlarged, nontender prostate. Urinalysis demonstrates pyuria and positive nitrites.

Vignette:
A 66-year-old woman presents with 2 days of progressive abdominal distension, diffuse crampy abdominal pain, and intractable vomiting that has become bilious and feculent. She has not passed flatus or had a bowel movement for 36 hours. Her surgical history includes an open appendectomy 30 years ago and a total abdominal hysterectomy 15 years ago. On examination, she appears dehydrated and in moderate distress. Vital signs: T 37.8C, HR 110, RR 20, BP 108/68, SpO2 97%. Abdomen is markedly distended and tympanitic with high-pitched tinkling bowel sounds. There is diffuse tenderness, greatest in the periumbilical region, with mild involuntary guarding. Labs: WBC 14,800/mcL, BUN 42, creatinine 1.6, lactate 3.1 mmol/L. CT abdomen demonstrates dilated small bowel loops up to 5.2 cm with a discrete transition point in the right lower quadrant with a small bowel feces sign and possible closed-loop configuration.

Vignette:
A 40-year-old male construction worker is extricated by rescue crews after being trapped under a collapsed concrete wall at a building site for approximately 4 hours. Both lower extremities were pinned. Upon extrication, he is alert and reports severe pain in both legs and a sensation of numbness. He has no significant past medical history. On examination, both lower extremities are markedly swollen, tense, and ecchymotic from the thighs to the ankles. Vital signs: T 36.4C, HR 118, RR 24, BP 96/62, SpO2 95%. Pedal pulses are weak bilaterally. Sensation is diminished throughout both legs. He reports dark brown urine since a Foley catheter was placed in the field, with only 50 mL output over the past 2 hours. Labs drawn immediately: potassium 6.8 mEq/L, creatinine 3.4 mg/dL, CK 124,000 U/L, phosphorus 7.6 mg/dL, calcium 6.2 mg/dL, uric acid 14.2 mg/dL, myoglobin 48,000 ng/mL, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, lactate 6.8 mmol/L. ECG shows peaked T waves. Aggressive IV normal saline resuscitation at 1.5 L/hr with sodium bicarbonate supplementation is initiated, along with continuous cardiac monitoring and IV calcium gluconate for cardioprotection.

Vignette:
A 47-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of the worst headache of her life that began 1 hour ago while straining during a bowel movement. She describes it as a thunderclap headache reaching maximum intensity within seconds. She experienced one episode of vomiting and brief loss of consciousness. Her past medical history includes migraines and she is a current smoker. On examination, she is photophobic, irritable, and has a stiff neck. Vital signs: T 37.4C, HR 96, RR 18, BP 178/96, SpO2 98%. Neurological exam reveals intact cranial nerves, mild bilateral lower extremity weakness, and pronounced nuchal rigidity. Hunt and Hess grade III. Non-contrast CT head reveals diffuse subarachnoid hemorrhage in the basal cisterns. CT angiography identifies a 7 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm.

Vignette:
A 5-month-old baby boy presents with difficulty and delay in passing hard stools. His mother reports that he strains for several hours and may even miss a day, before passing stool with screaming and occasional spots of fresh blood on the stool or diaper. He has recently been weaned from breastfeeding to cows' milk formula, which he had been reluctant to drink initially. The child is thriving and now feeding normally. There was no neonatal delay in defecation and no history of excessive vomiting or abdominal distension.

Vignette:
A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency department with acute onset of SOB of 30 minutes' duration. Initially, he felt faint but did not lose consciousness. He is complaining of left-sided chest pain that worsens on deep inspiration. He has no history of cardiopulmonary disease. A week ago he underwent a total left hip replacement and, following discharge, was on bed rest for 3 days due to poorly controlled pain. He subsequently noticed swelling in his left calf, which is tender on examination. His current vital signs reveal a fever of 100.4°F (38.0°C), heart rate 112 bpm, BP 95/65, and an O2 saturation on room air of 91%.

Vignette:
A 32-year-old woman at 34 weeks gestation (G3P2) presents with sudden onset of painful vaginal bleeding and severe constant abdominal pain that began 30 minutes ago. She has a history of chronic hypertension managed with labetalol and a prior placental abruption with her second pregnancy. She reports the baby's movements have decreased since the bleeding started. On examination, she is anxious, pale, and in significant distress. Vital signs: T 36.8C, HR 124, RR 24, BP 96/62, SpO2 96%. The uterus is firm, tender, and contracted (woody consistency) with no relaxation between contractions. Moderate dark red vaginal bleeding is present. Continuous fetal monitoring reveals a baseline fetal heart rate of 170 bpm with absent variability and repetitive late decelerations. Labs: hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL, platelets 108,000/mcL, fibrinogen 142 mg/dL (low), PT 14.8 seconds, D-dimer >20,000 ng/mL. Transfusion is initiated and emergent cesarean delivery is called.

Vignette:
A 30-year-old man presents to the urgent care clinic with a 6-hour history of severe pain, tearing, and foreign body sensation in his left eye. He was grinding metal at work without wearing safety goggles when he felt something strike his eye. Since then, he has had constant sharp pain, profuse tearing, photophobia, and difficulty keeping the eye open. He denies any change in vision other than blurriness from tearing. He wears contact lenses but removed them immediately after the incident. On examination, visual acuity is 20/30 in the left eye (baseline 20/20) and 20/20 in the right. There is conjunctival injection of the left eye with no hypopyon or hyphema. The pupil is round and reactive. Fluorescein staining under cobalt blue light reveals a 3 mm linear epithelial defect on the central cornea. Seidel test is negative. There is no retained foreign body visible on slit lamp examination or eversion of the upper lid.

Vignette:
A 68-year-old man presents with sudden onset of severe pain, coldness, and numbness in his left leg that started approximately 3 hours ago while sitting at home. He has a history of atrial fibrillation and was recently taken off warfarin due to a GI bleed. On examination, the left leg is pale and cool to the touch from the mid-thigh distally. Vital signs: T 36.9C, HR 88 (irregularly irregular), RR 16, BP 148/86, SpO2 97%. Left dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are absent by palpation and Doppler. Left popliteal pulse is faintly detectable. The left calf is tender with decreased sensation and the patient is unable to dorsiflex or plantarflex the left foot. Right leg pulses are palpable and symmetric. CT angiography shows abrupt occlusion of the left superficial femoral artery.

Vignette:
An 8-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after pulling a pot of boiling water off the stove onto himself approximately 45 minutes ago. He sustained scald burns to his anterior chest, abdomen, both upper extremities, and portions of his face. He has been crying inconsolably. He has no significant past medical history. On examination, he is alert but in severe pain and distress. Vital signs: T 36.6C, HR 152, RR 28, BP 94/58, SpO2 98%. Weight is 28 kg. Burns cover approximately 20% total body surface area: areas of erythema with large intact and ruptured blisters (superficial partial thickness) on the chest and abdomen, with waxy white insensate areas (deep partial to full thickness) on both forearms. No circumferential burns are identified. Facial burns are superficial with no singed nasal hairs and no evidence of inhalation injury. He has no hoarseness or stridor. Parkland formula is calculated (20% TBSA x 28 kg x 4 mL = 2,240 mL LR over first 24 hours), IV access is obtained, and morphine is administered for pain.

Vignette:
A 29-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician reporting 8 months of near-constant excessive worry about multiple domains of her life including work performance, finances, health, and her children's safety. She describes an inability to control the worry despite recognizing it is disproportionate. She reports associated restlessness, muscle tension predominantly in her neck and shoulders, difficulty falling asleep, irritability, and difficulty concentrating during meetings. She has tried meditation and exercise with only partial benefit. She denies panic attacks, specific phobias, obsessive thoughts, or traumatic experiences. She has no prior psychiatric history and takes no medications. She drinks one cup of coffee daily. Vital signs are normal. Physical examination reveals bilateral trapezius muscle tightness but is otherwise unremarkable. Thyroid function tests are within normal limits. GAD-7 score is 16 indicating severe anxiety.

Vignette:
A 40-year-old woman presents with a 2-year history of persistent nasal congestion, frequent sneezing, and clear rhinorrhea. She notes that symptoms are present year-round but worsen when she vacuums or dusts her home. She denies any history of asthma, wheezing, or shortness of breath. She has tried over-the-counter antihistamines intermittently with partial relief. On examination, nasal mucosa is pale and boggy bilaterally. There is a transverse nasal crease. No nasal polyps are visualized. Lungs are clear to auscultation. She lives in an older home with carpeted bedrooms and reports no pets.

Vignette:
A 16-year-old female high school student presents with complaints of fever, sore throat, and fatigue. She started feeling sick 1 week ago. Her symptoms are gradually getting worse, and she has difficulty swallowing. She has had a fever every day, and she could hardly get out of bed this morning. She does not remember being exposed to anybody with a similar illness recently. On physical examination she is febrile and looks sick. Enlarged cervical lymph nodes, exudative pharyngitis with soft palate petechiae and faint erythematous macular rash on the trunk and arms are found.

Vignette:
A 4-year-old boy is brought in by his parents after 6 hours of rapidly progressive sore throat, difficulty swallowing, and noisy breathing. He has had no significant past medical history and immunizations are not up to date (parents declined some vaccines). On examination, the child is sitting upright in a tripod position, leaning forward with his neck extended and jaw thrust forward. He is drooling profusely and appears anxious and toxic-appearing. Vital signs: T 39.8C, HR 162, RR 34, SpO2 92% on room air. Inspiratory stridor is audible without a stethoscope. His voice is muffled and he refuses to speak or drink. A soft tissue lateral neck X-ray obtained reveals a thumb sign consistent with epiglottic swelling. Anesthesiology and ENT are urgently called for airway management.

Vignette:
A 35-year-old man is referred by his primary care physician for psychiatric evaluation after presenting with a 2-month history of persistent low mood, loss of interest in activities he previously enjoyed including playing guitar and socializing, insomnia with early morning awakening, decreased appetite with an unintentional 14-pound weight loss, difficulty concentrating at work, and pervasive feelings of worthlessness. He describes his mood as an overwhelming heaviness that does not lift. He has been increasingly isolating from friends and family. He denies suicidal ideation, hallucinations, or delusions. He has no prior psychiatric history. He went through a significant relationship breakup 3 months ago. Vital signs are normal. On mental status examination, he is casually dressed with poor grooming. Psychomotor retardation is present. Speech is soft and slow. Affect is flat. Thought process is linear but impoverished. PHQ-9 score is 22 indicating severe depression.

Vignette:
A 72-year-old man presents with 3 days of vague periumbilical discomfort that has gradually localized to the right lower quadrant. He reports decreased appetite, mild nausea, and one episode of loose stool. His past medical history includes type 2 diabetes, coronary artery disease, and a total knee replacement. On examination, he is afebrile at 37.2C but appears mildly uncomfortable. Vital signs: HR 92, RR 18, BP 134/78, SpO2 97%. Abdominal exam reveals mild right lower quadrant tenderness without guarding or rebound. WBC is only mildly elevated at 11,200/mcL. CT abdomen with contrast shows a dilated appendix measuring 14 mm with periappendiceal fat stranding and a small contained fluid collection suggestive of early perforation.

Vignette:
A 29-year-old male software developer presents with eye fatigue, dryness, and a mild headache that worsens throughout the workday. He spends 10 to 12 hours daily in front of computer screens and often forgets to take breaks. He reports that symptoms improve on weekends when he reduces screen time. He denies blurred vision, floaters, flashes of light, or eye pain. He does not wear corrective lenses. On examination, visual acuity is 20/20 bilaterally. Extraocular movements are intact. Pupils are equal and reactive. Conjunctivae are mildly injected. The anterior segment and fundoscopic exams are normal bilaterally.

Vignette:
A 56-year-old woman with a history of smoking presents to her primary care physician with shortness of breath and cough for several days. Her symptoms began 3 days ago with rhinorrhea. She reports a chronic morning cough productive of white sputum, which has increased over the past 2 days. She has had similar episodes each winter for the past 4 years. She has smoked 1 to 2 packs of cigarettes per day for 40 years and continues to smoke. She denies hemoptysis, chills, or weight loss and has not received any relief from over-the-counter cough preparations.

Vignette:
A 25-year-old woman presents with 3 days of clear nasal discharge, mild sore throat, and occasional sneezing. She works as a daycare teacher and reports several children in her class have had similar symptoms. She denies fever, cough, dyspnea, ear pain, or facial pressure. On examination, temperature is 37.0°C. The oropharynx shows mild erythema without exudates. Nasal mucosa is mildly edematous with clear discharge. Tympanic membranes are normal bilaterally. Cervical lymph nodes are not enlarged. She is well-appearing and in no distress.

Vignette:
A 5-year-old boy is brought in by his mother who noticed multiple itchy red bumps on his arms and legs after he spent the afternoon playing outside in the backyard. The bumps appeared over the past 24 hours. He has been scratching but the mother reports no significant swelling beyond the immediate area of each bump. He denies fever, joint pain, or any recent travel. On examination, there are approximately 8 to 10 small erythematous papules, each 3 to 5 mm in diameter, scattered on the bilateral forearms and lower legs. Several have small central puncta. There is no surrounding cellulitis, lymphangitis, or regional lymphadenopathy.

Vignette:
A 24-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of dysuria and urinary frequency that has progressed to right flank pain, fever, and rigors over the past 24 hours. She reports nausea and one episode of vomiting. She has had two previous urinary tract infections in the past year treated with antibiotics. She is sexually active and uses oral contraceptives. She denies vaginal discharge or hematuria. Vital signs show temperature 102.2°F, heart rate 104, blood pressure 108/66, respiratory rate 18. On examination, she appears flushed and mildly uncomfortable. There is significant right costovertebral angle tenderness on percussion. Abdominal exam reveals mild suprapubic tenderness without guarding. Urinalysis shows large leukocyte esterase, positive nitrites, many white blood cells, and bacteria. A point-of-care pregnancy test is negative.

Vignette:
A 77-year-old man reports a 5-day history of burning and aching pain on the right side of his chest. This is followed by the development of erythema and a maculopapular rash in this painful area, accompanied by headache and malaise. The rash progressed to develop clusters of clear vesicles for 3 to 5 days, evolving through stages of pustulation, ulceration, and crusting.

Vignette:
A 28-year-old woman with known epilepsy is brought in by ambulance after her roommate witnessed continuous generalized tonic-clonic seizure activity for approximately 12 minutes. EMS administered 10 mg of intramuscular midazolam en route, but seizure activity persisted. Her past medical history includes focal epilepsy diagnosed at age 16, treated with levetiracetam. Her roommate reports she recently missed several doses of medication due to insurance issues. On arrival, she remains in continuous generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Vital signs: T 39.2C, HR 142, RR (irregular, 8-30), BP 168/98, SpO2 88% on non-rebreather mask. She is cyanotic around the lips. Finger-stick glucose is 142 mg/dL. IV lorazepam 4 mg is administered with brief cessation of convulsive activity, but seizures resume within 2 minutes.

Vignette:
A 31-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 6-month history of nipple discharge. She
has noticed that her breasts are tender and both nipples produce milky discharge on applying
mild pressure. She has not noted any bloody or clear nipple discharge, breast lumps, or skin
changes. She also states she has not had a menstrual period for 6 months, and her periods had
been irregular for 8 months before they stopped altogether. Prior to her menstrual irregularities,
her menses occurred at a normal frequency and duration. She is sexually active with a single
partner and is trying to conceive.

Review of Systems:
General: Gradually increasing lethargy over the past 2 months. 3 kg unintentional weight gain in
the past 6 months.

Skin: No rash or history of excessive facial hair or acne.

HEENT: No rhinorrhea, tinnitus, vertigo, or change in hearing.

Pulmonary: Noncontributory

Cardiovascular: Noncontributory

Gastrointestinal: Noncontributory

Genitourinary: Noncontributory

Gynecologic: Decreased libido. Vaginal dryness during sexual intercourse. She has been trying
to conceive for the last 2 years. One full-term, uncomplicated pregnancy 5 years ago.

Musculoskeletal: Noncontributory

Neurologic: 6-month history of dull frontal and occasionally retro-orbital headaches that are
increasing in frequency and that now occur almost daily and affect her work performance. There
are no associated neurologic symptoms, including disturbances of vision, strength, balance, or
gait. She denies nausea, photophobia, or phonophobia. Until 1 month ago, the headaches
would resolve completely with nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs, but for the last month taking
simple analgesia does not suffice. She denies history of headaches prior to 6 months ago.

Psychiatric: She is mildly depressed recently, which she attributes to the frequent headaches.
No suicidal ideation.

Past Medical History:
Medical history: She had mild asthma in childhood, which she outgrew. She has a 5-year-old
son after an uncomplicated pregnancy with spontaneous vertex delivery at 40 weeks.

Surgical history: No previous operations.

Medications: Acetaminophen 1 g daily as needed; ibuprofen 400 mg daily as needed. Ibuprofen
recently increased to as much as 400 to 600 mg twice daily.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Family history: Her father had a stroke in his 80s; mother had osteoporosis.

Social history: She eats a healthy balanced diet. She does not exercise regularly. She is
nonsmoker and drinks alcohol very occasionally. She works as a primary school teacher. Her
last travel outside the country was to Italy 8 months ago.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: Comfortable-appearing female who generally looks well and appears her
stated age.

Vital signs:
BMI: 22 kg/m2
Temperature: 36.6° C
Pulse: 80 beats/minute and regular
Respirations: 18/min
BP: 135/74 mm Hg

Pulmonary: Equal air entry and chest is clear on auscultation. No crackles or wheezes.

GYN: No breast masses or skin changes. No axillary lymphadenopathy. Mild diffuse breast

Vignette:
A 44-year-old woman with known Addison disease on chronic hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone replacement presents with 3 days of progressive nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain following a viral gastroenteritis illness. She has been unable to keep her oral medications down for 2 days. On examination, she is lethargic and appears critically ill with notable hyperpigmentation of the oral mucosa, palmar creases, and surgical scars. Vital signs: T 37.8C, HR 118, RR 22, BP 72/38 (unresponsive to 2L IV normal saline), SpO2 95%. Skin turgor is markedly decreased. Labs: sodium 118 mEq/L, potassium 6.4 mEq/L, glucose 52 mg/dL, BUN 48 mg/dL, creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, random cortisol 1.2 mcg/dL. ECG shows peaked T waves and prolonged PR interval. IV stress-dose hydrocortisone 100 mg is administered immediately.

Vignette:
A 55-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 11.2%) presents with rapidly worsening pain, swelling, and redness of his right lower leg that began 2 days ago after a minor abrasion he sustained while gardening. Despite oral cephalexin started by his PCP yesterday, the erythema has expanded dramatically. On examination, he appears toxic and diaphoretic. Vital signs: T 39.8C, HR 128, RR 24, BP 92/56, SpO2 95%. The right leg demonstrates tense, dusky erythema extending from the ankle to the knee with areas of purplish discoloration and hemorrhagic bullae. Crepitus is palpable along the anterior shin. Pain is severe and extends beyond the visible margins of erythema. Labs: WBC 28,200/mcL, glucose 428 mg/dL, sodium 131 mEq/L, creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, CRP 32 mg/dL, lactate 4.6 mmol/L. LRINEC score is 10. CT of the leg shows extensive gas tracking along the fascial planes.

Vignette:
A 20-year-old male college athlete presents with itchy, peeling skin between his toes bilaterally for the past 2 weeks. He plays on the soccer team and uses communal showers at the athletic facility daily. He denies pain, swelling, or spreading beyond the interdigital spaces. He has no history of diabetes or immunosuppression. On examination, there is maceration and peeling of the skin in the third and fourth interdigital web spaces of both feet. Mild erythema is present. There are no vesicles, bullae, or fissures extending to the soles. Toenails appear normal.

Vignette:
A 14-year-old boy presents with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Eighteen hours earlier, he had been at a picnic where he ingested undercooked chicken along with a variety of other foods. He reports moderate-volume, nonbloody stools occurring 6 times a day. He has mild abdominal cramps and a low-grade fever. He is evaluated at an acute care clinic and found to be mildly tachycardic (heart rate 105 bpm) with a normal BP and a low-grade temperature of 100.1°F (37.8°C). His physical exam is unremarkable except for mild diffuse abdominal tenderness and mild increased bowel sounds. He is able to take oral fluids and is instructed on the appropriate oral fluid and electrolyte rehydration.

Vignette:
A 28-year-old woman presents with a 9-month history of chronic watery diarrhea, abdominal bloating, and unintentional weight loss of 12 pounds. She reports 3 to 5 loose stools daily and intermittent crampy abdominal pain. She has also noticed increasing fatigue and occasional mouth sores. Her past medical history is unremarkable except for iron deficiency anemia diagnosed 6 months ago that has been poorly responsive to oral iron supplementation. On examination, she appears thin with a BMI of 18.5. She is pale. Abdominal examination reveals mild diffuse tenderness without organomegaly. There are no skin rashes. Laboratory results show hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL with a low MCV of 72, ferritin 8 ng/mL, and low serum vitamin D at 15 ng/mL. Tissue transglutaminase IgA antibody is elevated at 98 units (normal less than 20). Total IgA level is normal.

Vignette:

episode of confusion. The day prior to her visit she attended a wedding at which she had "2 or
3" glasses of wine and afterwards felt extremely tired whereby she left early. When she got
home, she went straight to bed without even undressing. She awoke about 3 h later and didn't
remember going to bed or that she had just been at a wedding. Both arms were painful when
she awoke, and she noticed blood in her mouth. Her husband says she had been "tossing
around in bed." She returned to bed and awoke in the morning several hours past her usual
time. She and her husband thought these events were very unusual, and although she felt back
to normal except for some slight soreness in her arms, she decided to go the emergency
department.

Review of Systems:

change.

HEENT: Mild discomfort and swelling on left lateral aspect of tongue.

Pulmonary: No shortness of breath or cough.

Cardiovascular: No chest pain, palpitations or edema, no difficulty doing her usual activities.

Gastrointestinal: Chronic constipation which has been stable for years, no abdominal pain,
nausea, or vomiting.

during sleep the prior night. No episodes of urinary incontinence prior to the current episode.

Musculoskeletal: Mild, diffuse bilateral upper extremity discomfort.

Neurologic: No headache, no vision changes, no neck stiffness, dizziness, or vertigo. No
weakness or loss of sensation.

Vignette:
A 38-year-old woman presents with a 3-week history of persistent throat clearing and a mild cough that is worse when lying down at night. She reports a sensation of mucus dripping in the back of her throat. She recently had a mild cold that resolved 4 weeks ago. She denies fever, facial pain, purulent nasal discharge, wheezing, or heartburn. She is a non-smoker. On examination, the oropharynx shows a cobblestone appearance of the posterior pharyngeal wall. Nasal mucosa is mildly erythematous with clear thin secretions. Lungs are clear to auscultation. There is no sinus tenderness on palpation.

Vignette:
A 19-year-old tall, thin male (6'3", 145 lbs) presents with sudden onset of sharp right-sided pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea that began 2 hours ago while playing basketball. He has no prior medical history, takes no medications, and does not smoke. On examination, he is mildly tachypneic but speaking in full sentences. Vital signs: T 36.8C, HR 104, RR 22, BP 128/76, SpO2 93% on room air. The right hemithorax is hyperresonant to percussion with decreased breath sounds on the right compared to the left. Chest X-ray reveals a large right-sided pneumothorax with approximately 60% lung collapse and no mediastinal shift. There is no evidence of pleural effusion.

Vignette:
A 50-year-old woman presents with a 5-day history of persistent dizziness described as a sensation of spinning. She reports the dizziness is constant rather than positional and is accompanied by an unsteady gait and difficulty walking in a straight line. She has had two episodes of nausea and vomiting. She denies hearing loss or tinnitus. Past medical history is notable for migraine headaches and hypertension. On examination, vital signs are stable. Neurological exam reveals vertical nystagmus that does not suppress with fixation, mild dysmetria on finger-to-nose testing on the right, and gait ataxia with veering to the right. Hearing is intact bilaterally. Dix-Hallpike maneuver is negative.

Vignette:
Mr. A is a 24 year-old man who presents to your office for complaints of sore throat, fever, and headache. His symptoms started 2 days ago with acute onset of sore throat and fever to 102.2. He has had no cough. His physical examination is normal, except for the presence of tonsillar exudates and some tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy. He is otherwise in good health, and is on no medications except for ibuprofen for fever. He has no drug allergies. (, Centor score = 4 – treat, or test and treat)

Vignette:
A 19-year-old man presents with a 5-day history of severe sore throat that has progressively worsened despite 3 days of oral amoxicillin prescribed for pharyngitis. He now reports difficulty swallowing and has been unable to eat solid food for 2 days. He describes a muffled "hot potato" voice and difficulty fully opening his mouth. He has been drooling due to pain with swallowing. He denies respiratory difficulty. Vital signs show temperature 101.4°F, heart rate 98, blood pressure 124/78. On examination, there is trismus with limited mouth opening to approximately 2 cm. Intraoral exam reveals a bulging, erythematous soft palate on the left with displacement of the left tonsil medially and inferiorly. The uvula is deviated to the right. There is tender left anterior cervical and submandibular lymphadenopathy. Lung auscultation is clear and there is no stridor.

Vignette:
A 30-year-old man presents with a 1-week history of mildly itchy, erythematous patches on both hands. He recently switched to a new laundry detergent approximately two weeks ago. He denies any history of atopic dermatitis, asthma, or food allergies. On examination, there are bilateral, symmetric, well-demarcated erythematous plaques on the dorsal hands with mild scaling. The skin is intact with no cracking, vesicles, or weeping. There is no involvement of the wrists or forearms. He works as an accountant and reports no occupational chemical exposures.

Vignette:
A 28-year-old woman presents with a 1-day history of nausea, three episodes of watery non-bloody diarrhea, and mild diffuse abdominal cramping. She reports her roommate had similar symptoms earlier in the week. She is able to tolerate oral fluids and has been sipping water and electrolyte drinks throughout the day. She denies fever, bloody stool, severe abdominal pain, or dizziness. On examination, vital signs are stable. The abdomen is soft with mild diffuse tenderness, no guarding or rebound. Mucous membranes are moist. Bowel sounds are hyperactive.

Vignette:
A 60-year-old woman presents with 5 days of progressive shortness of breath following a confirmed influenza A infection. Despite oseltamivir initiated 3 days ago, her respiratory status has continued to deteriorate. She has a history of well-controlled type 2 diabetes and obesity (BMI 38). On examination, she is in marked respiratory distress. Vital signs: T 38.9C, HR 118, RR 34, BP 106/62, SpO2 82% on high-flow nasal cannula at 60L/min and FiO2 100%. Lung auscultation reveals diffuse bilateral crackles. Chest X-ray demonstrates bilateral diffuse alveolar opacities consistent with pulmonary edema, but echocardiogram shows normal left ventricular function with no evidence of volume overload. ABG: pH 7.22, pO2 58, pCO2 52, PaO2/FiO2 ratio 58. She is intubated for mechanical ventilation.

Vignette:
A 32-year-old woman who is 4 months postpartum presents with a 6-week history of pain along the radial (thumb) side of her right wrist. The pain began insidiously and has progressively worsened. She attributes it to the repetitive motions of lifting and holding her infant. The pain is sharp and radiates proximally into the forearm and distally into the thumb. She reports difficulty gripping objects, turning her wrist, and making a fist. She is right-hand dominant. On examination, there is tenderness and mild swelling over the radial styloid process and the first dorsal compartment. Finkelstein test is markedly positive, reproducing sharp pain along the radial wrist when the thumb is grasped in a fist and the wrist is ulnarly deviated. Grip strength is reduced due to pain. Thumb range of motion is preserved but painful at extremes. Neurovascular examination of the hand is intact. Wrist radiographs are normal.

Vignette:
A 62-year-old man with chronic kidney disease stage 4 (baseline GFR 22) on maintenance hemodialysis presents after missing his last two dialysis sessions due to transportation issues. He reports 2 days of progressive generalized weakness, muscle cramps, and palpitations. He has continued to eat his usual diet, including bananas and orange juice. On examination, he appears fatigued and mildly short of breath. Vital signs: T 36.6C, HR 52 (irregular), RR 20, BP 172/96, SpO2 95%. Lower extremity exam reveals 2+ bilateral pitting edema and diminished deep tendon reflexes. Labs: potassium 7.8 mEq/L, BUN 112 mg/dL, creatinine 11.4 mg/dL, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, phosphorus 8.2 mg/dL. ECG demonstrates absent P waves, widened QRS complexes (duration 180 ms), and peaked T waves with a sine wave pattern beginning to emerge. IV calcium gluconate is administered emergently.

Vignette:
A 15-year-old girl presents with her mother for evaluation of bumps on her forehead and chin that have been present for the past 3 months. She reports they are not painful but she finds them cosmetically bothersome. She has been washing her face with regular soap twice daily. She denies any cystic lesions, scarring, or use of new cosmetics. Menarche was 1 year ago and her cycles are regular. She takes no medications. On examination, there are scattered open and closed comedones on the forehead and chin numbering approximately 15 to 20. A few small inflammatory papules, each less than 5 mm, are noted on the chin. There are no nodules, cysts, or scarring.

Vignette:
A 52-year-old obese man with a BMI of 36 presents for evaluation after his wife noticed he has been drinking large amounts of water and urinating frequently over the past several weeks. He reports increased thirst, frequent nighttime urination disrupting sleep, and a 10-pound unintentional weight loss over 2 months. He also describes blurry vision and increased fatigue. His past medical history includes hypertension treated with lisinopril and hyperlipidemia. Family history is significant for type 2 diabetes in both parents. He works a sedentary desk job and does not exercise regularly. Vital signs show blood pressure 144/92, heart rate 78. On examination, he is obese with acanthosis nigricans on the posterior neck and axillae. Foot examination shows intact sensation to monofilament and palpable pedal pulses. Fasting plasma glucose is 210 mg/dL, and HbA1c is 9.2%. Urinalysis shows glucosuria without ketonuria.

Vignette:
A 52-year-old woman with a 10-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with a 3-month history of progressively worsening stiffness and pain in her left shoulder. The pain is deep and aching, worse at night, and has made it increasingly difficult to reach behind her back, comb her hair, and fasten her bra. She denies any preceding trauma or injury. Her diabetes is managed with metformin and her last HbA1c was 7.8%. On examination, there is globally restricted active and passive range of motion of the left shoulder. External rotation is limited to 20 degrees (compared to 70 degrees on the right). Abduction is limited to 80 degrees, and internal rotation is severely restricted. There is no tenderness over specific rotator cuff tendons. Strength testing is limited by pain and stiffness. Shoulder radiographs show no fracture or dislocation and mild osteopenia.

Vignette:
A 40-year-old man with a known history of chronic rhinosinusitis and bilateral nasal polyps presents with a 10-day history of worsening facial pressure, purulent nasal discharge, nasal congestion, and anosmia. He has had recurrent sinus infections averaging four to five times per year and has previously undergone polypectomy two years ago. He reports postnasal drip and a productive cough worse at night. He denies fever, visual changes, or severe headache. On examination, the nasal mucosa is edematous and erythematous bilaterally with visible polypoid tissue and mucopurulent drainage in the middle meatus. There is tenderness over the maxillary and frontal sinuses. Oropharynx shows cobblestoning of the posterior pharyngeal wall.

Vignette:
A 35-year-old male teacher presents with 2 days of nasal congestion, frequent sneezing, mild sore throat, and a low-grade temperature of 37.6°C. He reports several students in his classroom have been out sick recently. He notes mild fatigue but denies cough, dyspnea, myalgias, or ear pain. On examination, the nasal turbinates are mildly swollen with clear discharge. The oropharynx is mildly erythematous without tonsillar enlargement or exudates. Tympanic membranes are clear. Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. He is well-hydrated and in no acute distress.

Vignette:
A 35-year-old man presents with 3 days of progressive bilateral submandibular and sublingual swelling, worsening trismus, odynophagia, and a muffled "hot potato" voice. Five days ago, he had a lower left second molar extracted at a dental clinic. He has no significant past medical history. On examination, he is sitting upright and drooling, appearing anxious and in respiratory distress. Vital signs: T 38.8C, HR 114, RR 24, BP 138/82, SpO2 91% on room air. There is firm, woody, bilateral submandibular swelling with erythema and warmth. The floor of the mouth is elevated and indurated, displacing the tongue posteriorly and superiorly. He is unable to fully open his mouth. Inspiratory stridor is audible. CT neck with contrast demonstrates a multiloculated fluid collection in the submandibular and sublingual spaces bilaterally with significant airway narrowing at the level of the oropharynx.

Vignette:

Her partner reports she has complained of a persistent headache, visual disturbances described as flashing lights, and swelling of her face and hands over the past 2 days. She did not attend her last two prenatal appointments. On examination, she is postictal, moaning, and not following commands. Vital signs: T 37.6C, HR 112, RR 22, BP 182/116, SpO2 94%. Significant periorbital and bilateral upper extremity edema is present. Deep tendon reflexes are 4+ bilaterally with sustained clonus at the ankles. Fetal heart rate monitoring shows persistent late decelerations. Labs: platelets 92,000/mcL, AST 286 U/L, ALT 312 U/L, LDH 680 U/L, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 5.2. IV magnesium sulfate is initiated and emergent cesarean delivery is planned.

Vignette:

On examination, there is mild swelling over the lateral aspect of the right ankle with mild tenderness over the anterior talofibular ligament. There is no ecchymosis. Vignette:
A 28-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of severe left-sided pelvic pain and lightheadedness that began 45 minutes ago. She reports 7 weeks of amenorrhea and a positive home pregnancy test 5 days ago. She has a history of pelvic inflammatory disease and a prior left tubal ectopic pregnancy treated with methotrexate 2 years ago. On examination, she is pale, diaphoretic, and appears acutely ill. Vital signs: T 36.4C, HR 132, RR 24, BP 78/48, SpO2 97%. Abdominal exam reveals diffuse lower abdominal tenderness with peritoneal signs. Pelvic exam demonstrates cervical motion tenderness and a tender left adnexal mass. Quantitative beta-hCG is 4,200 mIU/mL. Bedside transvaginal ultrasound reveals an empty uterus, a complex left adnexal mass with ring-of-fire sign, and significant free fluid in the pelvis and Morison's pouch. Vignette:
A 42-year-old man presents with mild low back ache that developed after spending several hours gardening yesterday. He was bending and lifting bags of soil. The pain is localized to the lower back and does not radiate to the legs. He denies numbness, tingling, weakness, or changes in bowel or bladder function. He has no history of prior back surgery or chronic back problems. On examination, there is mild paraspinal muscle tenderness in the lumbar region bilaterally. Range of motion is mildly reduced on flexion. Straight leg raise is negative bilaterally. Neurological examination of the lower extremities is normal.

Vignette:
A 35-year-old man who jogs regularly presents with a 1-week history of an itchy rash in his groin folds. He reports the itch worsens after running and sweating. He denies any genital lesions, urinary symptoms, or prior similar episodes. On examination, there are bilateral, well-demarcated erythematous plaques with slightly raised scaly borders along the inguinal creases extending to the proximal inner thighs. The scrotum is spared. There is no central clearing or satellite lesions. No inguinal lymphadenopathy is appreciated.

Vignette:
A 22-year-old female soccer player presents to the sports medicine clinic two days after sustaining a left knee injury during a game. She reports that while pivoting to change direction she felt a sudden pop in her knee followed by immediate swelling and inability to continue playing. She was unable to bear full weight and has been using crutches since. She denies any prior knee injuries. On examination, there is a moderate effusion of the left knee. Range of motion is limited by pain and swelling. The Lachman test is positive with a soft endpoint on the left, and the anterior drawer test demonstrates increased anterior tibial translation compared to the right. McMurray test is equivocal. The collateral ligaments are stable. She is neurovascularly intact distally.

Vignette:
A 6-year-old boy is brought to his pediatrician by his mother who noticed patches of hair loss on his scalp over the past 3 weeks. The patches have been gradually enlarging and the affected areas appear scaly. He attends elementary school and his mother reports several classmates have had similar issues. He denies pain but admits to mild itching. On examination, there are two well-defined round patches of alopecia on the parietal and occipital scalp, measuring approximately 3 cm and 2 cm in diameter respectively. Within the patches, the hair shafts are broken off at the surface giving a black-dot appearance. The surrounding scalp is covered with fine gray-white scale. There is mild posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. A Wood lamp examination reveals no fluorescence. KOH preparation of plucked hairs shows endothrix spores surrounding and within the hair shaft.

Vignette:
A 9-year-old boy is brought to the ER after being stung by a bee at a picnic. He is crying hysterically. After 15 minutes of calming him down, exam reveals a swollen tender upper lip but no tongue swelling, no drooling, no stridor, no rash, and no other complaints.

Vignette:
A 32-year-old woman presents with a 10-month history of recurrent episodes of abdominal cramping and altered bowel habits. She describes lower abdominal pain that is relieved with defecation, alternating between periods of diarrhea lasting several days and constipation lasting a week. Symptoms worsen during periods of work-related stress. She denies blood in her stool, nocturnal symptoms, fever, or weight loss. Family history is negative for inflammatory bowel disease or colorectal cancer. On examination, vital signs are normal. She appears anxious but in no acute distress. Abdominal examination reveals mild tenderness in the left lower quadrant with a palpable sigmoid colon on deep palpation. No masses, organomegaly, or guarding. Rectal examination is normal. Complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, C-reactive protein, and thyroid function tests are within normal limits. Stool calprotectin is negative.

Vignette:

On examination, there is a tense, bluish-purple, spherical, tender nodule approximately 2 cm in diameter at the anal verge, consistent with a thrombosed external hemorrhoid. There is surrounding mild edema but no erythema suggesting infection. Digital rectal exam is deferred due to pain.

On further questioning it is revealed that he has significant eye itching, redness, and tearing as well as palate and throat itching during the spring season. He remembers that his mother told him at some point that he used to have eczema in infancy.

Vignette:
A 30-year-old woman presents in January with 2-day history of fever, cough, headache, and generalized weakness. She was in her usual state of health before an abrupt onset of these symptoms. A few viral illnesses have affected her during the current winter, but not to this severity. She reports sick contacts at work and did not receive the seasonal influenza vaccine this season.

Vignette:

On examination, a small non-tender, soft, external perianal skin tag approximately 5 mm is noted at the 6 o'clock position. There is no thrombosis, bleeding, prolapse, or surrounding erythema.

Vignette:
A 16-year-old male competitive swimmer presents with a 4-day history of progressive right ear pain and itching. He has been swimming daily for the past 3 weeks during summer training. The pain worsens when he chews food and when he lies on his right side. He reports a sensation of fullness in the ear and mild hearing reduction. He denies fever, ear discharge, or recent upper respiratory symptoms. On examination, vital signs are normal. There is marked tenderness on manipulation of the right tragus and with traction on the right auricle. Otoscopic examination reveals a narrowed, edematous external auditory canal with erythematous, macerated skin and scant white debris. The tympanic membrane is barely visible but appears intact. The left ear examination is normal. There is no periauricular lymphadenopathy, mastoid tenderness, or facial nerve dysfunction.

Vignette:
A 35-year-old female office worker presents with a dull, bilateral headache described as a band-like pressure around her head. The headache started in the late afternoon after a long day of meetings and computer work. She rates the pain as 4 out of 10. She denies nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, or visual changes. There is no aura. She reports similar headaches occurring a few times per month for the past year. On examination, vital signs are normal. There is mild tenderness of the bilateral temporal and occipital muscles on palpation. Neurological examination is entirely normal. Fundoscopic exam is unremarkable.

Vignette:
A 25-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician after experiencing her fourth episode in the past 6 weeks of sudden-onset palpitations, shortness of breath, chest tightness, diaphoresis, trembling, and an intense fear of dying. The episodes reach peak intensity within minutes and typically last 15 to 30 minutes before gradually subsiding. Between episodes she has developed significant anticipatory anxiety and has begun avoiding crowded places such as shopping malls and public transportation. She has presented to the emergency department twice during episodes, where cardiac workup including ECG, troponin, and chest radiograph were normal. She has no medical history and no family history of cardiac disease. Vital signs today are normal. Physical examination is unremarkable. Thyroid function tests, CBC, and basic metabolic panel are normal. A 24-hour Holter monitor showed sinus tachycardia during one symptomatic episode only.

Vignette:
A 30-year-old man presents with 2 days of loose watery stools, occurring 3 to 4 times per day, since returning from a vacation in Mexico. He denies blood or mucus in the stool, fever, or vomiting. He reports mild abdominal cramping that is intermittent and not severe. He is maintaining adequate oral hydration. He has no significant past medical history. On examination, vital signs are normal. The abdomen is soft, non-tender, with active bowel sounds. There are no signs of dehydration. He appears well and is in no distress.

Vignette:
A 12-year-old boy is brought in by his mother after experiencing a brief nosebleed from his left nostril approximately 30 minutes ago. The bleeding lasted about 5 minutes and stopped with firm pinching of the nose. His mother reports the house has been very dry due to winter heating, and she has noticed him picking his nose frequently. He denies any history of easy bruising, prolonged bleeding from cuts, or prior nosebleeds requiring medical attention. On examination, there is a small dried blood clot visible at the anterior septum of the left nostril. No active bleeding is noted. The remainder of the nasal exam is normal.

Vignette:
A 38-year-old man with no significant history of back pain developed acute LBP when lifting boxes 2 weeks ago. The pain is aching in nature, located in the left lumbar area, and associated with spasms. He describes previous similar episodes several years ago, which resolved without seeing a doctor. He denies any leg pain or weakness. He also denies fevers, chills, weight loss, and recent infections. Over-the-counter ibuprofen has helped somewhat, but he has taken it only twice a day for the past 3 days because he does not want to become dependent on painkillers. On examination, there is decreased lumbar flexion and extension secondary to pain, but a neurologic exam is unremarkable.

Vignette:
A 45-year-old man presents with the complaint that he has not had a bowel movement in 5 days. He works a sedentary office job and admits to a diet low in fruits, vegetables, and fiber. He drinks approximately 3 cups of coffee daily but only 2-3 glasses of water. He denies abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, blood in stool, or unintentional weight loss. He has no prior surgical history. On examination, the abdomen is soft, non-distended, with mild fullness palpable in the left lower quadrant. Bowel sounds are present and normal.

Vignette:
A 6-year-old boy with a medical history significant for mild persistent asthma is brought to the clinic by his mother with a history of a 5-day cough. His mother reports that the child's fever continues to be elevated despite acetaminophen therapy. He has missed school for the past 3 days and he has a classmate sick with pneumonia. The mother reports that the appetite is good for the child. His cough produced yellowish sputum at home. His vitals at the clinic are: respiratory rate 19 breaths/min, heart rate 80 beats/min, and temperature 101.6°F (38.7°C). He appears in no respiratory distress. His lung examination reveals bilateral rales and occasional wheeze. CXR reveals lobar infiltrates without pleural effusions.

Vignette:
A 30-year-old woman, 10 days postpartum after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery, presents with sudden-onset right-sided pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath that began 2 hours ago while breastfeeding. She reports mild right calf swelling for the past 3 days that she attributed to normal postpartum changes. On examination, she is tachypneic and anxious. Vital signs: T 37.3C, HR 118, RR 26, BP 98/62, SpO2 91% on room air. Right calf is 3 cm larger in circumference than the left with a palpable cord. Lungs are clear. D-dimer is elevated at 4,200 ng/mL. CT pulmonary angiography reveals bilateral segmental and subsegmental pulmonary emboli with right heart strain.

Vignette:
A 22-year-old man is brought in by EMS after a high-speed motorcycle collision 15 minutes ago. He was wearing a helmet but was thrown from the bike and struck a guardrail on the right side. On arrival, he is in severe respiratory distress, gasping for air, and unable to speak in full sentences. Vital signs: T 36.4C, HR 138, RR 36, BP 74/48, SpO2 78% on 15L non-rebreather mask. Neck veins are distended and the trachea is deviated to the left. Right hemithorax is hyperresonant to percussion with absent breath sounds. Left lung has normal breath sounds. Subcutaneous emphysema is palpable along the right chest wall and neck. Needle decompression is performed at the right 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line, with an immediate rush of air.

Vignette:
A 48-year-old overweight male mail carrier with a BMI of 31 presents with a 2-month history of sharp stabbing pain in the bottom of his right heel. The pain is most severe with the first few steps in the morning and after standing up from prolonged sitting, then gradually improves with activity but returns after extended periods of walking on his mail route. He walks approximately 8 miles daily on pavement. He wears standard-issue work boots without orthotic inserts. He denies any trauma, numbness, tingling, or night pain. On examination, there is exquisite point tenderness over the medial calcaneal tubercle at the origin of the plantar fascia. Pain is reproduced with passive dorsiflexion of the toes (windlass test). Achilles tendon is nontender and intact. Heel fat pad is unremarkable. There is tightness of the gastrocnemius-soleus complex bilaterally. Neurovascular examination is intact. Weight-bearing lateral foot radiograph shows a small calcaneal spur, which is noted to be an incidental and common finding.

Vignette:

Vignette:
A 38-year-old female office worker presents with a 6-week history of pain over the outer aspect of her right elbow. She works at a computer for 8 to 10 hours daily and recently increased her keyboard and mouse usage during a major project. The pain worsens with gripping activities such as opening jars, turning doorknobs, and shaking hands. She denies trauma, swelling, or locking of the elbow. On examination, there is point tenderness over the lateral epicondyle of the right elbow. Pain is reproduced with resisted wrist extension and resisted middle finger extension (Maudsley test). Grip strength is reduced on the right compared to the left. Range of motion of the elbow is full and painless. There is no joint instability or effusion. Neurovascular examination is normal.

Vignette:
A 45-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician with a 6-month history of progressive fatigue, weight gain of 15 pounds despite no change in diet, constipation, cold intolerance, and dry skin. She reports her hair has become thin and brittle and she has noticed puffiness around her eyes in the morning. Her menstrual periods have become heavier and more irregular. She has no significant past medical history and takes no medications. Family history is positive for thyroid disease in her mother and sister. Vital signs show heart rate 56, blood pressure 136/88, temperature 97.2°F. On examination, she appears sluggish. Skin is cool, dry, and pale. There is periorbital edema and non-pitting edema of the lower extremities. The thyroid gland is diffusely enlarged without nodules. Deep tendon reflexes show delayed relaxation phase. TSH is markedly elevated at 48 mIU/L and free T4 is low at 0.4 ng/dL. Anti-TPO antibodies are positive.

Vignette:
A 48-year-old woman with a history of migraine headaches presents to the emergency room with altered mental status over the last several hours. She was found by her husband, earlier in the day, to be acutely disoriented and increasingly somnolent. On physical examination, she has scleral icterus, mild right upper quadrant tenderness, and asterixis. Preliminary laboratory studies are notable for a serum ALT of 6498 units/L, total bilirubin of 5.6 mg/dL, and INR of 6.8. Her husband reports that she has consistently been taking pain medications and started taking additional 500 mg acetaminophen pills several days ago for lower back pain. Further history reveals a medication list with multiple acetaminophen-containing preparations.

Vignette:

Vignette:
A 68-year-old woman who has followed a strict vegan diet for the past 12 years presents with a 4-month history of progressive tingling and numbness in both feet, fatigue, and difficulty with balance. She reports her tongue has been sore intermittently. She has noticed increased forgetfulness and mild cognitive slowing. She takes no supplements. On examination, vital signs are normal. She appears pale with a smooth, beefy red tongue (glossitis). Neurological examination reveals diminished vibration and proprioception in both feet and ankles, absent ankle reflexes, and a positive Romberg sign. Gait is wide-based and mildly ataxic. Upper extremity neurological exam is normal. CBC reveals hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL with an MCV of 112 fL. Peripheral blood smear shows macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils. Serum B12 level is critically low at 85 pg/mL (normal 200-900). Methylmalonic acid and homocysteine levels are both elevated.

Vignette:
A 42-year-old woman presents with 8 hours of severe, constant epigastric pain radiating straight through to the back, rated 9/10. The pain began after a fatty meal and is associated with persistent nausea and multiple episodes of vomiting. She has a history of cholelithiasis diagnosed 6 months ago but declined elective cholecystectomy. On examination, she is lying very still with her knees drawn up. Vital signs: T 38.2C, HR 116, RR 22, BP 96/58, SpO2 96%. Abdomen is tender in the epigastrium with guarding but no rebound. Bowel sounds are diminished. Labs: lipase 2,840 U/L (normal <60), WBC 16,200/mcL, AST 210 U/L, ALT 185 U/L, total bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL, calcium 7.8 mg/dL. Vignette:
An 18-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents with 4 days of profuse watery diarrhea (10-12 episodes daily) and vomiting (6-8 episodes daily). On examination, the infant is limp and lethargic with a weak, barely audible cry. Vital signs: T 38.2C, HR 182, RR 32, BP 68/38 (hypotensive for age), capillary refill 5 seconds. The anterior fontanelle is markedly sunken. Eyes appear deeply sunken with absent tears. Mucous membranes are parched. Skin tenting persists for more than 3 seconds when pinched. Weight is 9.8 kg (previous weight at well-child visit 2 weeks ago was 11.2 kg, representing a 12.5% weight loss). Labs: sodium 158 mEq/L, potassium 2.8 mEq/L, BUN 42 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL (elevated for age), bicarbonate 12 mEq/L, glucose 62 mg/dL. IV normal saline bolus 20 mL/kg is initiated.

Vignette:

Vignette:
A 12-year-old girl presents with sudden-onset severe generalized abdominal pain associated with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. On exam she appears ill and has a temperature of 104°F (40°C). Her abdomen is tense with generalized tenderness and guarding. No bowel sounds are present.

Vignette:
A 30-year-old man presents with a painful, swollen right eye for the past day. He reports minor pain on palpation of the eyelid and denies any history of trauma, crusting, or change in vision. He has no history of allergies or any eye conditions and denies the use of any new soaps, lotions, or creams. On exam, he has localized tenderness to palpation and erythema on the midline of the lower eyelid near the lid margin. The remainder of the physical exam, including the globe, is normal.

Vignette:
A 78-year-old man is brought in after a syncopal episode at home witnessed by his wife. She reports he has been increasingly fatigued and lightheaded for the past week. His past medical history includes aortic stenosis, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes. On examination, he is alert but pale and mildly confused. Vital signs: T 36.6C, HR 32, RR 18, BP 82/50, SpO2 93%. Cannon A waves are visible in the jugular venous pulse. Heart sounds reveal a systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border and variable intensity of S1. ECG demonstrates complete atrioventricular dissociation with a ventricular escape rate of 32 bpm, wide QRS complexes, and independent P waves at a rate of 82 bpm.

He had been traveling in Central America for 3 months, returning 8 weeks ago. He had been bitten by mosquitoes on multiple occasions, and although he initially took malaria prophylaxis, he discontinued it due to mild nausea. He does not know the specifics of his prophylactic therapy. On examination he has a temperature of 100.4°F (38°C), and is mildly tachycardic with a BP of 126/82 mmHg. The remainder of the examination is normal.

Vignette:
A 56-year-old man presents to urgent care with acute onset of excruciating pain in his right great toe that woke him from sleep at 3 AM. The pain developed rapidly over several hours and is now the worst pain he has ever experienced, rated 10 out of 10. He reports the toe is so sensitive that even the weight of a bedsheet is unbearable. He had a steak dinner with several beers the evening before onset. His past medical history includes hypertension managed with hydrochlorothiazide and hyperlipidemia. He is overweight with a BMI of 30. On examination, the right first metatarsophalangeal joint is intensely erythematous, swollen, warm, and exquisitely tender to even light palpation. Active and passive range of motion is severely limited by pain. Vital signs show temperature 99.4°F, heart rate 88. Serum uric acid is 9.8 mg/dL. Inflammatory markers show ESR 42 and CRP 6.2.

Vignette:
A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes managed with glipizide and metformin is found confused and diaphoretic on his living room floor by his daughter. She reports he has had poor oral intake for the past 2 days due to a gastrointestinal illness with vomiting and diarrhea but continued taking all medications. On examination by EMS, he is obtunded, drenched in sweat, and exhibiting intermittent tremors. Vital signs: T 35.8C, HR 108, RR 20, BP 162/94, SpO2 96%. Finger-stick glucose reads 28 mg/dL. Neurological exam shows bilateral extensor plantar responses, generalized hyperreflexia, and no focal deficits. EMS administers 25 g of dextrose 50% IV with improvement in mental status within minutes, but glucose subsequently drops again to 42 mg/dL, requiring a continuous dextrose 10% infusion.

Vital signs: T 38.4C, HR 112, RR 28, BP 108/68, SpO2 88% on room air. Lung auscultation reveals bilateral diffuse crackles. Chest X-ray shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates with a ground-glass pattern. LDH is markedly elevated at 580 U/L. Induced sputum is sent for silver stain.

The lower gingiva is mildly swollen and erythematous over the area of the central incisors, and a tooth bud is palpable beneath the surface. The remainder of the exam is normal.

Between episodes she notes persistent mild tinnitus and a sense that her right ear hearing has gradually deteriorated. She experiences nausea and sometimes vomiting during attacks. She denies headache, visual changes, or focal neurological symptoms. Audiometry demonstrates low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss in the right ear with normal hearing on the left. On examination between episodes, vital signs are normal. The Rinne test shows air conduction greater than bone conduction bilaterally. Weber test lateralizes to the left ear. Neurological exam is nonfocal.

He is otherwise in good health, and is on no medications except for acetaminophen for his sore throat and fever. He has no drug allergies.

Vignette:
A 15-year-old girl presents with a superficial scrape on her left knee after falling off her skateboard approximately 1 hour ago. She was wearing shorts and fell onto pavement. She cleaned the wound with water at home. She denies hitting her head, loss of consciousness, or any other injuries. Her tetanus immunization is up to date. On examination, there is a 6 by 4 cm superficial abrasion on the anterior left knee with minor oozing of serous fluid. There is no active arterial bleeding, no embedded foreign material visible, and no involvement of deeper tissue. The surrounding skin is intact. Range of motion of the knee is full and painless.

Vignette:
A 65-year-old man with hypertension and degenerative joint disease presents to the emergency department with a three-day history of a productive cough and fever. He has a temperature of 38.3°C (101°F), a blood pressure of 144/92 mm Hg, a respiratory rate of 22 breaths per minute, a heart rate of 90 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation of 92 percent while breathing room air. Physical examination reveals only crackles and egophony in the right lower lung field. The white-cell count is 14,000 per cubic millimeter, and the results of routine chemical tests are normal. A chest radiograph shows an infiltrate in the right lower lobe.

Vignette:
A 33-year-old man presents with a several-month history of persistent flaky, scaly patches on his scalp and eyebrows. He reports mild itching that is worse after showering. He has tried regular shampoo without improvement. He denies hair loss, spreading to other body areas, or any joint symptoms. He has no history of psoriasis or HIV. On examination, there are yellowish, greasy scales on the scalp, particularly along the hairline and in the eyebrow region. Mild erythema underlies the scales. There are no excoriations or signs of secondary infection.

Vignette:
A 3-year-old boy is brought in by his mother after 6 days of persistent high fever unresponsive to acetaminophen and ibuprofen. Over the past several days, she has noticed redness in both eyes without discharge, a rash on his trunk, swelling of his hands and feet, cracked bleeding lips, and a red bumpy tongue. He has been increasingly irritable and refusing to eat. On examination, the child is febrile, irritable, and difficult to console. Vital signs: T 39.6C, HR 148, RR 28, BP 86/52. Bilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection is present. Lips are erythematous with fissures. A prominent strawberry tongue is noted. A diffuse polymorphous maculopapular rash covers the trunk and perineum with early desquamation in the groin. Bilateral hands and feet show indurative edema with erythema. Right anterior cervical lymphadenopathy measuring 2.0 cm is palpable. Labs: WBC 18,600/mcL, ESR 82 mm/hr, CRP 12.4 mg/dL, albumin 2.6 g/dL, platelets 488,000/mcL, ALT 68 U/L. Echocardiogram reveals dilated left anterior descending coronary artery (z-score 3.2). IVIG and high-dose aspirin are initiated.

Vignette:
A 30-year-old man who describes himself as an avid gamer presents with a dull ache in his right wrist that has been gradually worsening over the past 2 weeks. The pain is worse during and after prolonged gaming sessions and improves with rest. He denies any specific injury, swelling, numbness, or locking of the wrist. He is right-hand dominant. On examination, the right wrist has full range of motion. There is mild tenderness along the dorsal extensor tendons without visible swelling or erythema. Finkelstein test is negative. Grip strength is mildly reduced compared to the left. Neurovascular exam is intact.

Vignette:

treated in the past for chronic sinusitis and asthma. A year ago, she had balloon rhinoplasty to
enlarge her sinuses. Today, she says that she first noticed the nasal-sounding voice a week
after surgery, but it has become more apparent over the last 3 mo.
Today, she says it feels as though air escapes through her nose while speaking, giving it a
nasal quality. Her voice is better in the morning and worse later in the day. She says she does
not have dysphagia but notes occasional nasal regurgitation of liquids but not food. She denies
diplopia, drooping eyelids, loss of smell or taste, and difficulty with balance or gait. She denies
having arm and leg weakness and numbness.
