Test (units) Result
Color: Yellow pH: 5.8
Specific gravity 1.010
RBCs: 0-2/hpf WBCs: 0-1/hpf
Leukocyte esterase: Negative
Nitrites: Negative
Bacteria: Negative

Doppler ultrasonography of scrotum:
Heterogeneous-appearing left testis, with no demonstrated venous or arterial Doppler blood flow. Normal-appearing right testis with normal venous and arterial blood flow.

Vignette:
A 17-year-old male student presents with recurrent mouth ulceration since his early schooldays. He has no respiratory, anogenital, gastrointestinal, eye, or skin lesions. His mother had a similar history as a teenager. The social history includes no tobacco use and virtually no alcohol consumption. He has no history of recent drug or medication ingestion. Extraoral exam reveals no significant abnormalities and specifically no pyrexia

Vignette:
A 42-year-old man with a history of Crohn disease managed with azathioprine presents with a 3-day history of burning pain along the left side of his chest followed by the eruption of grouped vesicles on an erythematous base. The rash follows a band-like distribution along the T5 dermatome and does not cross the midline. He reports associated malaise and low-grade fever. Vital signs are stable with temperature 99.8°F. On examination, there are clustered vesicles in various stages, some with clear fluid and others beginning to crust. There is notable allodynia in the affected dermatome. No ocular or facial involvement is present.

Vignette:
A 12-year-old girl presents with sudden-onset severe generalized abdominal pain associated with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. On exam she appears ill and has a temperature of 104°F (40°C). Her abdomen is tense with generalized tenderness and guarding. No bowel sounds are present.

Vignette:
A 30-year-old man presents with a painful, swollen right eye for the past day. He reports minor pain on palpation of the eyelid and denies any history of trauma, crusting, or change in vision. He has no history of allergies or any eye conditions and denies the use of any new soaps, lotions, or creams. On exam, he has localized tenderness to palpation and erythema on the midline of the lower eyelid near the lid margin. The remainder of the physical exam, including the globe, is normal.

Vignette:
A 78-year-old man is brought in after a syncopal episode at home witnessed by his wife. She reports he has been increasingly fatigued and lightheaded for the past week. His past medical history includes aortic stenosis, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes. On examination, he is alert but pale and mildly confused. Vital signs: T 36.6C, HR 32, RR 18, BP 82/50, SpO2 93%. Cannon A waves are visible in the jugular venous pulse. Heart sounds reveal a systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border and variable intensity of S1. ECG demonstrates complete atrioventricular dissociation with a ventricular escape rate of 32 bpm, wide QRS complexes, and independent P waves at a rate of 82 bpm.

Vignette:
A 28-year-old man presents to his physician with a 5-day history of fever, chills, and rigors, not improving with acetaminophen (paracetamol), along with diarrhea. He had been traveling in Central America for 3 months, returning 8 weeks ago. He had been bitten by mosquitoes on multiple occasions, and although he initially took malaria prophylaxis, he discontinued it due to mild nausea. He does not know the specifics of his prophylactic therapy. On examination he has a temperature of 100.4°F (38°C), and is mildly tachycardic with a BP of 126/82 mmHg. The remainder of the examination is normal.

Vignette:
A 56-year-old man presents to urgent care with acute onset of excruciating pain in his right great toe that woke him from sleep at 3 AM. The pain developed rapidly over several hours and is now the worst pain he has ever experienced, rated 10 out of 10. He reports the toe is so sensitive that even the weight of a bedsheet is unbearable. He had a steak dinner with several beers the evening before onset. His past medical history includes hypertension managed with hydrochlorothiazide and hyperlipidemia. He is overweight with a BMI of 30. On examination, the right first metatarsophalangeal joint is intensely erythematous, swollen, warm, and exquisitely tender to even light palpation. Active and passive range of motion is severely limited by pain. Vital signs show temperature 99.4°F, heart rate 88. Serum uric acid is 9.8 mg/dL. Inflammatory markers show ESR 42 and CRP 6.2.

Vignette:
A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes managed with glipizide and metformin is found confused and diaphoretic on his living room floor by his daughter. She reports he has had poor oral intake for the past 2 days due to a gastrointestinal illness with vomiting and diarrhea but continued taking all medications. On examination by EMS, he is obtunded, drenched in sweat, and exhibiting intermittent tremors. Vital signs: T 35.8C, HR 108, RR 20, BP 162/94, SpO2 96%. Finger-stick glucose reads 28 mg/dL. Neurological exam shows bilateral extensor plantar responses, generalized hyperreflexia, and no focal deficits. EMS administers 25 g of dextrose 50% IV with improvement in mental status within minutes, but glucose subsequently drops again to 42 mg/dL, requiring a continuous dextrose 10% infusion.

Vignette:
A 34-year-old male with a history of HIV (CD4 count 45 cells/mcL, not on antiretroviral therapy) presents with a 2-week history of progressive dyspnea, dry cough, and low-grade fevers. He reports significant fatigue and an unintentional 10-pound weight loss over the past month. On examination, he appears cachectic and is in mild respiratory distress. Vital signs: T 38.4C, HR 112, RR 28, BP 108/68, SpO2 88% on room air. Lung auscultation reveals bilateral diffuse crackles. Chest X-ray shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates with a ground-glass pattern. LDH is markedly elevated at 580 U/L. Induced sputum is sent for silver stain.

Vignette:
A 7-month-old girl is brought in by her parents who report she has been unusually fussy for the past 3 days. They have noticed increased drooling and that she constantly chews on her fingers and toys. She is eating slightly less than usual but still taking adequate formula. She has no fever, no diarrhea, and no rash. On examination, temperature is 37.0°C. The infant is mildly irritable but consolable. The lower gingiva is mildly swollen and erythematous over the area of the central incisors, and a tooth bud is palpable beneath the surface. The remainder of the exam is normal.

Vignette:
A 48-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of recurrent episodes of severe spinning vertigo lasting 2 to 4 hours per episode, occurring approximately twice monthly. Each episode is preceded by a sensation of fullness in her right ear and accompanied by roaring tinnitus and reduced hearing on the right side. Between episodes she notes persistent mild tinnitus and a sense that her right ear hearing has gradually deteriorated. She experiences nausea and sometimes vomiting during attacks. She denies headache, visual changes, or focal neurological symptoms. Audiometry demonstrates low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss in the right ear with normal hearing on the left. On examination between episodes, vital signs are normal. The Rinne test shows air conduction greater than bone conduction bilaterally. Weber test lateralizes to the left ear. Neurological exam is nonfocal.

Vignette:
Mr. E is a 26 year-old man who presents to your office for complaints of sore throat, headache, and non-productive cough. His symptoms started 2 days ago with acute onset of sore throat. He has been afebrile. His physical examination is normal, except for some pharyngeal erythema. He is otherwise in good health, and is on no medications except for acetaminophen for his sore throat and fever. He has no drug allergies.

Vignette:
Mr. Y is a 64 year old Chinese male who presents with chest pain for 24 hours. One day prior to presentation, the patient began to experience 8/10, non-radiating substernal chest pressure associated with diaphoresis and shortness of breath. The pain intially improved with Tylenol, however over the following 24 hours, his symptoms worsened. The patient went to his primary physician, where an EKG was performed which showed ST elevation in leads V2-V6.

Vignette:
A 10-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of constant right-sided
scrotal pain. The pain began several hours prior to presentation and awoke him from sleep. He
is an otherwise healthy boy who states he has never experienced pain like this before. He
denies a history of genital trauma or any sexual activity, and he has not noticed any swelling or
lumps in his groin. He has not had any fevers, chills, urinary frequency, dysuria, hematuria, or
urethral discharge.

Review of Systems:
General: Denies subjective fevers or chills.

Skin: Denies itching and rashes or other lesions.

HEENT: Noncontributory

Pulmonary: Noncontributory

Cardiovascular: Denies palpitations, chest pain.

Gastrointestinal: Denies abdominal pain, diarrhea, constipation, nausea, or vomiting.

Genitourinary: No dysuria, hematuria, frequency, or urgency.

Musculoskeletal: Denies joint pain.

Neurologic: Denies numbness or paresthesias in any extremities.

Psychiatric: Noncontributory

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Eczema

Surgical history: Neonatal circumcision

Medications: Daily pediatric multivitamin

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Family history: Grandfather with hypertension.

Social history: He is currently in 4th grade; immunizations are up-to-date; not exposed to
tobacco smoke at home; no known sick contacts; has not traveled to any foreign countries.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: In mild distress due to pain.

Vital signs:
Temperature: 36.7° C
Pulse: 87 beats/min
BP: 123/68 mm Hg

Respirations: 16/min
Height: 137 cm
Weight: 32 kg

Skin: Warm and dry to the touch, no rashes.

HEENT: Normocephalic, atraumatic.

Pulmonary: Breath sounds present and equal bilaterally. No stridor, no rales, no wheezing.

Cardiovascular: Regular heart rate and rhythm, no murmurs, radial pulses are present and
equal bilaterally.

Gastrointestinal: Abdomen is flat, no visible lesions, bowel sounds normal. On palpation,
abdomen is soft, nontender, no guarding, no masses.

Genitourinary: Circumcised phallus, no urethral discharge or lesions, no scrotal swelling or
erythema. Testes normal size, no masses.

Musculoskeletal: No costovertebral angle tenderness.

Neurologic: Unremarkable

Mental status: Alert and oriented to person, place, time, and event.

Test Results:
Appropriate testing is ordered and results are shown:

Urinalysis: Normal

Doppler ultrasonography of the scrotum: 8 x 5 mm microcystic lesion adjacent to the right epididymal head. There is no significant flow within or surrounding the lesion. The testes appear normal bilaterally with appropriate arterial and venous flow.

Vignette:
A 15-year-old girl presents with a superficial scrape on her left knee after falling off her skateboard approximately 1 hour ago. She was wearing shorts and fell onto pavement. She cleaned the wound with water at home. She denies hitting her head, loss of consciousness, or any other injuries. Her tetanus immunization is up to date. On examination, there is a 6 by 4 cm superficial abrasion on the anterior left knee with minor oozing of serous fluid. There is no active arterial bleeding, no embedded foreign material visible, and no involvement of deeper tissue. The surrounding skin is intact. Range of motion of the knee is full and painless.

Vignette:
A 65-year-old man with hypertension and degenerative joint disease presents to the emergency department with a three-day history of a productive cough and fever. He has a temperature of 38.3°C (101°F), a blood pressure of 144/92 mm Hg, a respiratory rate of 22 breaths per minute, a heart rate of 90 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation of 92 percent while breathing room air. Physical examination reveals only crackles and egophony in the right lower lung field. The white-cell count is 14,000 per cubic millimeter, and the results of routine chemical tests are normal. A chest radiograph shows an infiltrate in the right lower lobe.

Vignette:
A 33-year-old man presents with a several-month history of persistent flaky, scaly patches on his scalp and eyebrows. He reports mild itching that is worse after showering. He has tried regular shampoo without improvement. He denies hair loss, spreading to other body areas, or any joint symptoms. He has no history of psoriasis or HIV. On examination, there are yellowish, greasy scales on the scalp, particularly along the hairline and in the eyebrow region. Mild erythema underlies the scales. There are no excoriations or signs of secondary infection.

Vignette:
A 3-year-old boy is brought in by his mother after 6 days of persistent high fever unresponsive to acetaminophen and ibuprofen. Over the past several days, she has noticed redness in both eyes without discharge, a rash on his trunk, swelling of his hands and feet, cracked bleeding lips, and a red bumpy tongue. He has been increasingly irritable and refusing to eat. On examination, the child is febrile, irritable, and difficult to console. Vital signs: T 39.6C, HR 148, RR 28, BP 86/52. Bilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection is present. Lips are erythematous with fissures. A prominent strawberry tongue is noted. A diffuse polymorphous maculopapular rash covers the trunk and perineum with early desquamation in the groin. Bilateral hands and feet show indurative edema with erythema. Right anterior cervical lymphadenopathy measuring 2.0 cm is palpable. Labs: WBC 18,600/mcL, ESR 82 mm/hr, CRP 12.4 mg/dL, albumin 2.6 g/dL, platelets 488,000/mcL, ALT 68 U/L. Echocardiogram reveals dilated left anterior descending coronary artery (z-score 3.2). IVIG and high-dose aspirin are initiated.

Vignette:
A 30-year-old man who describes himself as an avid gamer presents with a dull ache in his right wrist that has been gradually worsening over the past 2 weeks. The pain is worse during and after prolonged gaming sessions and improves with rest. He denies any specific injury, swelling, numbness, or locking of the wrist. He is right-hand dominant. On examination, the right wrist has full range of motion. There is mild tenderness along the dorsal extensor tendons without visible swelling or erythema. Finkelstein test is negative. Grip strength is mildly reduced compared to the left. Neurovascular exam is intact.

Vignette:
A 48-yr-old woman comes to the office because of a nasal-sounding voice. She has been
treated in the past for chronic sinusitis and asthma. A year ago, she had balloon rhinoplasty to
enlarge her sinuses. Today, she says that she first noticed the nasal-sounding voice a week
after surgery, but it has become more apparent over the last 3 mo.
Today, she says it feels as though air escapes through her nose while speaking, giving it a
nasal quality. Her voice is better in the morning and worse later in the day. She says she does
not have dysphagia but notes occasional nasal regurgitation of liquids but not food. She denies
diplopia, drooping eyelids, loss of smell or taste, and difficulty with balance or gait. She denies
having arm and leg weakness and numbness.

Review of Systems:
General: She has generally felt well and has been able to do her usual activities. Since her
sinus surgery, she has had occasional shooting pains in the back of her head on the left occiput.

Skin: Noncontributory

HEENT: No nasal congestion or discharge.

Pulmonary: No dyspnea or wheezing.

Cardiovascular: No chest pain or palpitations.

Gastrointestinal: Good appetite, normal bowel movements, and no recent weight loss or gain.

Genitourinary: No difficulty starting or stopping urination and no incontinence. Last normal
menstrual period 3 wk ago.

Musculoskeletal: No extremity or joint pain. Normal perceived strength.

Neurologic: See previous screen (History of Present Illness).

Psychiatric: Normal mood, although she is beginning to be concerned about her vocal
symptoms.

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Asthma controlled by daily corticosteroid inhaler. Uses rescue bronchodilator 3
to 4 times/yr; last use was 2 mo ago. Sinusitis, with multiple episodes in the past, but none since
her sinus surgery.

Surgical history: Balloon rhinoplasty for sinus enlargement (1 yr ago).

Medications: Beclomethasone inhaler twice/day; albuterol inhaler as needed.

Allergies: Erythromycin

Family history: Negative

Social history: She eats a regular diet and does not exercise. There is no history of recent
travel. She denies drug, alcohol, and tobacco use. Immunizations are up to date, and there has
been no recent exposure to illness.

Physical Examination:

Vignette:
A 58-year-old woman with a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with a 2-day history of increasing pain, redness, and swelling of her right foot. She recalls stepping on a nail while walking barefoot in her yard four days ago. She cleaned the wound at the time but did not seek medical attention. She reports low-grade fever and mild chills. On examination, vital signs are temperature 100.6°F, heart rate 84, blood pressure 142/88. The right foot shows a puncture wound on the plantar surface with surrounding erythema extending 6 cm, warmth, edema, and tenderness. There is no crepitus or fluctuance. Peripheral pulses are diminished bilaterally. Her last tetanus booster was over 10 years ago.

Vignette:
A 28-year-old woman who is 3 weeks postpartum and exclusively breastfeeding presents with a 2-day history of increasing pain, redness, and swelling in her right breast. She reports associated fever and chills and feeling generally unwell. She had been experiencing nipple soreness and cracking on the right side and notes the baby has had difficulty latching on that side. She denies palpable masses or nipple discharge other than breast milk. Vital signs show temperature 101.2°F, heart rate 94, blood pressure 118/72. On examination, there is a wedge-shaped area of erythema, warmth, and induration in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast. The area is exquisitely tender to palpation. There is no fluctuance or palpable abscess. The ipsilateral nipple shows a small fissure. Axillary lymph nodes are mildly enlarged on the right.

Vignette:
A 22-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes diagnosed at age 8 presents with 2 days of worsening nausea, vomiting, diffuse abdominal pain, and progressive lethargy. She reports that she ran out of insulin 3 days ago and could not afford a refill. On examination, she is drowsy but arousable, markedly dehydrated with dry mucous membranes and poor skin turgor. Vital signs: T 36.4C, HR 128, RR 32 (deep, labored Kussmaul respirations), BP 92/54, SpO2 99%. Her breath has a distinct fruity acetone odor. Abdomen is diffusely tender without peritoneal signs. Labs: glucose 486 mg/dL, pH 7.08, pCO2 14 mmHg, bicarbonate 4 mEq/L, anion gap 32, beta-hydroxybutyrate 8.2 mmol/L, potassium 5.6 mEq/L (expected to drop with treatment), sodium 128 mEq/L (corrected 134), BUN 38 mg/dL, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL.

Vignette:
A 58-year-old man presents with sudden onset of severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back between his shoulder blades that began 45 minutes ago while lifting heavy boxes. He has a history of poorly controlled hypertension and takes amlodipine intermittently. On examination, he is writhing in pain and appears ashen. Vital signs: T 36.8C, HR 108, RR 24, BP 210/118 in the right arm and 162/90 in the left arm. A diastolic murmur is auscultated along the left sternal border. Pulses are diminished in the left upper extremity. Chest X-ray shows widened mediastinum. CT angiography of the chest reveals a Stanford type A dissection originating in the ascending aorta with an intimal flap extending into the aortic arch.

Vignette:
A 45-yr-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 6-h history of acute-onset
left-sided lower abdominal pain. He describes the pain as starting over his left flank and
radiating down toward his groin. The pain comes and goes but is intense when present. He has
had some mild nausea without vomiting. The pain does not change with eating. The pain is less
when he walks around than when he sits or lies down flat. He has not had any bloody stools,
black stools, or change in bowel habits. He denies having diarrhea and constipation. He has
noticed his urine looks "dark" but denies pain during urination and urinary frequency. He says
that he swims several times a week for exercise, and this pain started immediately after
swimming. He also notes that several days ago, his son ran into his left side while playing
football. He took some acetaminophen, which minimally relieved his discomfort. He now
presents for evaluation at the emergency department because the pain has not subsided. He
says he has never experienced pain like this.

Review of Systems:
General: Has otherwise felt well before onset of his current symptoms. Denies fevers, chills,
weight loss, and fatigue.

Skin: Denies rashes, itching, and any lesions.

HEENT: Noncontributory

Pulmonary: Noncontributory

Cardiovascular: Denies palpitations and chest pain. No lower-extremity edema.

Gastrointestinal: Reports nausea when pain is at its most intense but no vomiting. No
constipation or diarrhea. Last bowel movement yesterday; no hematochezia or melena. No
appetite; he has not eaten since the pain began.

Genitourinary: No dysuria, hematuria, urinary frequency or urgency, or increased volume of
urine. States urine appears "dark."

Musculoskeletal: Occasional low back pain with strenuous activity

Neurologic: Noncontributory

Psychiatric: Noncontributory

Past Medical History:
Diabetes mellitus since his 20s that is well-controlled with oral drugs, diet, and exercise.
Hypertension and hyperlipidemia both well-controlled on drugs. Obstructive sleep apnea for
which he uses a CPAP machine. Recent deep venous thrombosis that developed after a long
international flight and that is currently being treated with an oral anticoagulant. Denies history
of UTIs, difficulty with urination, COPD, renal stones, and immunosuppressive disorders.

Surgical history: Wisdom tooth extraction as a teenager; no abdominal surgical procedures.

Medications: Lisinopril 10 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily, rosuvastatin 10 mg daily, rivaroxaban
20 mg daily, metformin 850 mg daily, and niacin 1 g daily.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Family history: Mother and father have hypertension; sibling has history of kidney stones.

Social history: He denies current and previous tobacco use. He works at a desk job and swims
laps at his local pool several times a week. All immunizations are up-to-date. He denies
exposure to any sick contacts. For the past 15 yr, he has had unprotected sex only with his wife.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: Appears nontoxic but seems uncomfortable on the exam bed.

Vital signs:
Temperature: 37° C
Pulse: 99 beats/min
BP: 150/90 mm Hg
Respirations: 16/min
Height: 6 ft (1.83 m)

He is a non-smoker and has no history of asthma or chronic lung disease. He denies fever, hemoptysis, or significant sputum production. On examination, vital signs are within normal limits. Lungs reveal occasional scattered rhonchi that clear with coughing. There are no wheezes or crackles. Oxygen saturation is 98% on room air.

Vignette:
A 22-year-old sexually active man presents with a 4-day history of gradually worsening left scrotal pain and swelling. The pain is dull and aching and radiates to the left inguinal region. He reports mild dysuria and a small amount of urethral discharge noticed over the past week. He has had a new sexual partner in the past month and inconsistently uses barrier protection. He denies fever, nausea, vomiting, or testicular trauma. Vital signs are normal. On examination, the left hemiscrotum is swollen and erythematous. There is tenderness and induration localized to the left epididymis posterior to the testis. Prehn sign is positive with relief of pain on elevation of the left testis. The cremasteric reflex is present bilaterally. There is no testicular torsion on clinical assessment. Urinalysis shows 15 to 20 WBC per high-power field. A nucleic acid amplification test for chlamydia and gonorrhea is sent.

A 63-year-old man sustained a cut on his hand while gardening. His immunization history is significant for not having received a complete tetanus immunization schedule. He presents with signs of generalized tetanus with trismus ("lock jaw"), which results in a grimace described as "risus sardonicus" (sardonic smile). Intermittent tonic contraction of his skeletal muscles causes intensely painful spasms, which last for minutes, during which he retains consciousness. The spasms are triggered by external (noise, light, drafts, physical contact) or internal stimuli, and as a result he is at the risk of sustaining fractures or developing rhabdomyolysis. The tetanic spasms also produce opisthotonus, board-like abdominal wall rigidity, dysphagia, and apneic periods due to contraction of the thoracic muscles and/or glottal or pharyngeal muscles. During a generalized spasm the patient arches his back, extends his legs, flexes his arms in abduction, and clenches his fists. Apnea results during some of the spasms. Autonomic overactivity initially manifests as irritability, restlessness, sweating, and tachycardia. Several days later this may present as hyperpyrexia, cardiac arrhythmias, labile hypertension, or hypotension.

Vignette:

Vignette:
A 32-year-old woman with a history of Graves disease (non-compliant with methimazole for 2 months) presents with 2 days of palpitations, agitation, profuse sweating, and diarrhea. She had a dental extraction 3 days ago. On examination, she is markedly agitated, tremulous, and unable to remain still. Vital signs: T 40.0C (104F), HR 162 (atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response), RR 28, BP 168/60 (widened pulse pressure), SpO2 97%. She has a fine tremor, bilateral proptosis, lid lag, diffuse goiter with an audible bruit, and brisk reflexes throughout. Skin is warm and moist. She becomes increasingly confused during the examination. Labs: TSH <0.01 mIU/L, free T4 7.8 ng/dL (normal 0.8-1.8), free T3 22 pg/mL (normal 2.3-4.2). Vignette:
A 70-year-old man with a history of chronic HTN and atrial fibrillation is witnessed by a family member to have nausea, vomiting, and right-sided weakness, as well as difficulty speaking and comprehending language. The symptoms started with only mild slurred speech before progressing over several minutes to severe aphasia and right arm paralysis. The patient is taking warfarin.

Vignette:

She denies any blistering, weeping, or spreading of the rash beyond the areas of contact. She has no history of eczema or other skin conditions. On examination, there are well-demarcated erythematous patches on both wrists corresponding to where the bracelet sits. There is mild scaling but no vesiculation, excoriation, or secondary infection. The remainder of the skin exam is normal.

Vignette:
A 28-year-old woman presents with a cluster of small blisters on her lower lip that appeared today. She reports a tingling and burning sensation in the area that started yesterday. She has experienced similar episodes approximately twice a year for the past 5 years. She notes she has been under increased stress at work. She denies fever, sore throat, or oral ulcers. On examination, there is a cluster of small fluid-filled vesicles on an erythematous base on the left lower lip at the vermilion border. There is no facial nerve involvement, no lymphadenopathy, and no intraoral lesions.

Vignette:
A 50-year-old man presents with a 3-day history of worsening lower back pain radiating bilaterally to both legs, progressive bilateral leg weakness, and difficulty urinating since yesterday. He has a history of lumbar disc disease with two prior episodes of sciatica managed conservatively. On examination, he walks with a wide-based unsteady gait. Vital signs are within normal limits. Neurological exam reveals decreased strength (3/5) in bilateral ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, diminished patellar and absent Achilles reflexes bilaterally, and decreased perianal sensation with reduced anal sphincter tone on rectal exam. Vignette:
A 25-year-old woman presents with bilateral thigh soreness that began yesterday, approximately 36 hours after her first gym session involving squats and lunges. She has not exercised regularly before. The soreness is worse with movement, particularly going downstairs. She denies any acute injury, popping sensation, bruising, or swelling. She has no history of myopathy or rhabdomyolysis. On examination, both quadriceps and hamstrings are mildly tender to palpation bilaterally. There is no edema, ecchymosis, warmth, or joint effusion. Range of motion of both knees and hips is full, though mildly uncomfortable at end range. She ambulates normally.

Vignette:

She has a history of irregular menstrual periods and follows a restrictive diet. On examination, there is focal tenderness and mild soft-tissue swelling over the mid-shaft of the third metatarsal. Pain is elicited with the tuning fork test and with axial loading of the third toe. She has a BMI of 19. Foot radiographs obtained at another facility one week ago were normal.

Vignette:

There are numerous small erythematous papules and tiny vesicles clustered on the neck, upper chest, and skin folds. The infant is alert, active, and well-hydrated.

Vignette:
A 45-year-old male farmer is brought in by coworkers after collapsing in the field approximately 30 minutes after spraying crops with an organophosphate insecticide without adequate protective equipment. Her cough is disrupting her sleep pattern and as a consequence she is experiencing daytime somnolence, which is affecting her job performance.

Vignette:

Vignette:

There is no underlying erythema, no oozing, and no involvement of the face or diaper area. The infant is content and thriving.

Vignette:

Vital signs show temperature 101.8°F, heart rate 96, blood pressure 110/68, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. The fundal height is consistent with gestational age and fetal heart tones are reassuring at 145 bpm. Rapid influenza antigen test is positive for influenza A. She has no signs of respiratory distress or dehydration.

Vignette:
A 22-year-old male college student presents with a painful sore inside his mouth for the past 2 days. He is in the middle of final examinations and reports increased stress and poor sleep. He denies fever, multiple ulcers, genital sores, or joint pain. He has no history of inflammatory bowel disease. On examination, a single shallow oval ulcer approximately 5 mm in diameter is visible on the buccal mucosa of the left cheek. It has a white-yellowish base with an erythematous halo. The remainder of the oral exam is unremarkable. There is no lymphadenopathy.

Vignette:
A 68-year-old male farmer presents with a slowly growing lesion on his nose that he first noticed approximately 8 months ago. The lesion has gradually enlarged and occasionally bleeds when he washes his face but heals over. He has extensive sun exposure from decades of outdoor work and a history of multiple sunburns in his youth. He has never had skin cancer before. On examination, there is a 1.2 cm pearly, dome-shaped nodule on the left ala of the nose with a rolled border and central depression. Multiple telangiectasias are visible on the surface. The surrounding skin shows significant solar damage with actinic keratoses on the forehead and ears. There is no palpable cervical or preauricular lymphadenopathy. A dermoscopic examination reveals arborizing vessels and blue-gray ovoid nests.

Vignette:
A 62-year-old woman with a history of osteoarthritis managed with daily naproxen for the past 3 years presents with a 4-week history of gnawing epigastric pain, early satiety, and occasional nausea. Bowel sounds are normoactive. There is no hepatosplenomegaly. A fecal occult blood test is negative. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 12.1 g/dL.

Vignette:
A 34-year-old man presents to urgent care after twisting his left ankle while stepping off a curb earlier today. He describes an inversion mechanism and reports hearing a crack at the time of injury. Point tenderness is present over the distal fibula with palpable bony tenderness at the posterior edge of the lateral malleolus. The medial malleolus is nontender. Anterior drawer test of the ankle is difficult to assess due to pain and guarding. Neurovascular status of the foot is intact with brisk capillary refill and intact sensation. Ankle radiographs demonstrate a non-displaced transverse fracture of the distal fibula (Weber B) with no talar shift.

Vignette:
A 40-year-old man presents with difficulty falling and staying asleep over the past 5 nights. He recently took on a major project at work with a tight deadline and reports feeling anxious about it. He estimates sleeping only 4 to 5 hours per night and experiencing daytime fatigue and difficulty concentrating. He denies depressed mood, loss of interest in activities, or suicidal ideation. He has no history of sleep disorders. He consumes coffee until mid-afternoon. On examination, he is well-groomed but appears mildly fatigued. Vital signs are normal. Neurological exam and mental status exam are unremarkable.

Vignette:
A 5-year-old girl is brought to the clinic by her parents for a spreading rash around her mouth and nose that began 5 days ago. It started as a small red spot near her left nostril and has since developed into multiple crusty lesions. Several children at her daycare have had similar sores. She is otherwise well with no fever, sore throat, or decreased appetite. On examination, there are multiple well-defined erosions with thick golden-yellow (honey-colored) crusts clustered around the nares and upper lip, with two satellite lesions on the left cheek. The lesions range from 1 to 3 cm in size. There is no warmth, fluctuance, or deep tissue involvement. There is mild left submandibular lymphadenopathy. The remainder of the skin examination is normal. She has no history of eczema or immunodeficiency.

Vignette:

Vignette:
An 8-year-old girl is brought to the pediatrician by her mother for intense itching that has been worsening over the past 2 weeks. The itching is particularly severe at night and disrupts her sleep. Several short, linear burrows approximately 5 to 10 mm in length are visible in the web spaces between the fingers. The face and scalp are spared. There are no vesicles or bullae. A mineral oil preparation from a burrow scraping examined under microscopy reveals mites, eggs, and fecal pellets.

A 10-year-old girl is brought in by her parents who report she frequently feels nauseated and dizzy during car rides, particularly on winding roads. Symptoms have been occurring for the past year and typically resolve within 15 to 20 minutes after stopping the vehicle. She does not vomit. Sitting in the front seat and looking out the window helps somewhat. She denies hearing loss, tinnitus, headaches, or similar symptoms outside of car rides. On examination, she is well-appearing and in no distress. Vital signs are age-appropriate. Neurological exam, including cranial nerves and cerebellar testing, is normal. Otoscopic exam is unremarkable.

Vignette:
A 50-year-old man presents with intermittent burning sensation in the substernal area that he has experienced occasionally over the past several weeks. The burning typically occurs 30 to 60 minutes after large meals, particularly those that are spicy or high in fat. The discomfort is relieved within minutes by over-the-counter antacids. He denies dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, hematemesis, or melena. He has no cardiac history. On examination, vital signs are normal. The abdomen is soft, non-tender, and non-distended. There is no epigastric tenderness. Cardiac exam is unremarkable.

Vignette:
A 60-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of progressively worsening left lower quadrant abdominal pain that is constant and dull. She reports low-grade fever and mild nausea but no vomiting. She had a colonoscopy 2 years ago that showed extensive diverticulosis of the sigmoid colon. Her diet is low in fiber. She reports one episode of constipation followed by loose stools. Vital signs show temperature 100.8°F, heart rate 86, blood pressure 128/76. On examination, there is moderate tenderness in the left lower quadrant with voluntary guarding but no rebound tenderness or rigidity. Bowel sounds are present and hypoactive. There is no palpable mass. Laboratory work shows a white blood cell count of 13,200 with a left shift. CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast demonstrates sigmoid diverticulitis with pericolic fat stranding and no abscess or perforation.

Vignette:
A 12-year-old boy is brought to the office by his mother for a well-child checkup. The patient and his mother both state that the patient has been otherwise well except for occasional mild pain and stiffness in the upper back. Symptoms began gradually about a year ago and are present intermittently. The pain and stiffness do not bother him significantly or limit his activities, and they have never awakened him from sleep. He denies any trauma or overuse. He is not currently playing any organized sports although he is able to be normally active with friends and siblings.

Review of Systems:
General: Patient feels well except for occasional upper back pain and stiffness. No fever, chills, or night sweats. No weight loss or change in appetite. He is not yet shaving, and his voice has not yet changed.

Skin: Mild acne, no other rash or lesions.

HEENT: No vision changes, ear pain, hearing changes, neck stiffness, or pain in the throat.

Pulmonary: No shortness of breath or cough.

Cardiovascular: No chest pain or pressure.

Gastrointestinal: No diarrhea, vomiting, or abdominal pain. Normal bowel movement once a day.

Genitourinary: No dysuria or increased urinary frequency.

Musculoskeletal: Positive for intermittent upper back stiffness and discomfort. No joint swelling or discomfort.

Neurologic: No numbness, tingling, or pain running down his arms or legs. No weakness or gait changes. No difficulty controlling bladder or bowels.

Psychiatric: No depression, psychosis, or hyperactivity.

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Uncomplicated birth, no hospitalizations.

Surgical history: None

Medications: None

Allergies: Penicillin (rash)

Family history: His father had diabetes and hypertension and died when patient was very young. His maternal grandmother died of breast cancer at age 76 years. There is no history of skeletal dysplasia or muscular dystrophy in the family.

Social history: Patient was born at 37 weeks' gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery and had an uncomplicated postnatal course. He is in age-appropriate grade in school and doing well academically and behaviorally. On interview with the mother outside the room, the patient reports that he feels happy and supported at home with his mother and sisters. Patient reports that he has never tried alcohol, drugs, or cigarettes. He is not sexually active.

The patient's family is from Guinea Bissau but the patient was born and raised in the United States and has not traveled outside the country. No known history of tuberculosis exposure. He is up to date on all vaccinations, and he received an influenza vaccine this year. He eats a normal diet, including fruits and vegetables, and drinks milk daily.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: African-American male child in no apparent discomfort, normal build and appearance.

Height: 160 cm (92nd percentile), Weight: 40 kgs (47th percentile)

Vital signs:
Temperature: 37° C
Pulse: 80 beats/min
BP: 105/66 mm Hg
Respirations: 16/min

Skin: No lesions or abnormal markings.

HEENT: Moist mucous membranes, normal dentition, no caries. Eye examination and vision normal bilaterally. Hearing grossly normal.

Pulmonary: Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally. No chest deformity.

Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs, rubs, or gallops

Gastrointestinal: Abdomen soft, nontender, nondistended.

Genitourinary: Normal male genitalia Tanner Stage 3, testes descended bilaterally.

Musculoskeletal: Back has mild paraspinous tenderness bilaterally in the thoracic region. When patient bends forward at the waist with his arms hanging and palms together, his shoulders are not level and his scapulae appear asymmetric. Palpation of the spinous processes show slight right thoracic and left lumbar curvature. There is no leg-length discrepancy, and iliac crests are symmetrical. Extremities have full range of motion, no visible or palpable deformities or tenderness of extremities or joints.

Neurologic: Alert and oriented to person, place, and time. Normal patellar relaxes 2+ bilaterally, 5/5 motor strength in bilateral upper and lower extremities. Normal gait. No clonus. No strictures or rigidity in the extremities.

Mental status: Appropriate affect and behavior.

Test Results:
Results of appropriate testing return and show the following results:

X-ray of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine:

No bony lesions noted. No signs of sacroiliitis. Scoliosis is present with right thoracic deviation and left lumbar deviation, Cobb angle 11°.

Focused musculoskeletal examination results:

Joint hypermobility: Absent
Ratio of upper body to lower body: 1.06
Ratio of wingspan to height: 0.98

Vignette:
A 19-year-old female college student is brought in by her roommate with a 24-hour history of high fever, diffuse rash, vomiting, profuse watery diarrhea, and progressive lightheadedness. She reports using a menstrual tampon that she forgot to change for approximately 3 days. On examination, she appears acutely ill with a diffuse, blanching, erythematous macular rash resembling a sunburn covering the trunk and extremities, including the palms and soles. Vital signs: T 40.2C, HR 136, RR 26, BP 72/40, SpO2 94%. Mucous membranes are hyperemic. Pelvic exam reveals a retained tampon, which is removed, and there is no evidence of abscess. Labs: WBC 15,400/mcL, platelets 88,000/mcL, creatinine 2.8 mg/dL, AST 245 U/L, ALT 198 U/L, CK 1,240 U/L. Blood cultures are drawn and empiric clindamycin and vancomycin are initiated.

Vignette:
A 32-year-old male singer presents with a hoarse voice that has persisted for 3 days following an intense concert performance. He reports mild sore throat and throat dryness but denies dyspnea, stridor, dysphagia, fever, or hemoptysis. He is a non-smoker and does not consume alcohol regularly. He has no history of GERD or thyroid disease. On examination, he is afebrile. The oropharynx is mildly erythematous without exudates or lesions. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy. His voice is notably hoarse and breathy. Respiratory effort is normal with no stridor or wheezing on auscultation.

Vignette:
A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents after 8 hours of progressive wheezing and respiratory distress despite using his albuterol inhaler every 20 minutes at home. He has a history of moderate persistent asthma with two prior ICU admissions. He recently had an upper respiratory infection. On examination, he is sitting upright, using accessory muscles, and speaking in single words only. Vital signs: T 37.8C, HR 152, RR 42, BP 100/65, SpO2 87% on room air. Lung auscultation reveals markedly diminished breath sounds bilaterally with minimal wheezing, suggesting severe air trapping. Peak flow is unobtainable due to patient fatigue. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.28, pCO2 55 mmHg.

Vignette:
A 53-yr-old woman comes to the office because of palpitations. She is a current patient there
and has a history of well-controlled hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and tension headaches. She
states that she has noticed intermittent palpitations over the past 2 mo. She describes the
episodes as a sensation of irregular and racing heartbeats that are accompanied by fatigue.
She denies any chest pain, shortness of breath, light-headedness, or syncope. The episodes
last from 10 min to several hours, occur once or twice/wk, and resolve on their own. The last
episode was 3 days ago. She cannot identify any particular triggers. She is generally active and
walks 3 miles several days/wk without any exertional symptoms including chest pain and
dyspnea. She has no family history of early cardiac disease or sudden death. She denies any
recent fever or infectious symptoms.

Review of Systems:
General: Patient has generally been feeling fine.

Skin: No new rashes or skin lesions.

HEENT: No vision changes, ear pain, nasal symptoms, or sore throat.

Pulmonary: Denies shortness of breath, dyspnea during exertion, and cough.

Cardiovascular: No orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or lower-extremity edema.

Gastrointestinal: Denies abdominal pain and poor appetite.

Genitourinary: Noncontributory

Reproductive: Noncontributory

Musculoskeletal: No recent injury.

Neurologic: Noncontributory

Psychiatric: Has been generally in good spirits; no extremes of mood.

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and tension headaches.

Surgical history: Appendectomy at age 20.

Medications: Lisinopril 10 mg daily and metformin 500 mg bid.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Family history: Mother is alive and has hypertension and diabetes mellitus. Father died of lung
cancer. No history of early coronary artery disease or sudden cardiac death.

Social history: Patient is married and works as a school teacher. Regularly exercises 3
times/wk. No history of smoking. Drinks a glass of wine with dinner most nights and one cup of
coffee each morning. Denies use of decongestants, cocaine, and other stimulants. No illicit drug
use.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: Slender middle-aged woman in no apparent distress.

Vital signs:
Temperature: 37.2° C
Pulse: 58 beats/min
BP: 125/74 mm Hg
Respirations: 14/min
Oxygen saturation: 96% on room air

Skin: No rashes noted.

HEENT: Oropharynx clear.

Pulmonary: Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally. No wheeze, rhonchi, or rales.

Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Brisk carotid upstrokes. No jugular venous distention.

Gastrointestinal: Soft, nontender, nondistended abdomen; positive bowel sounds.

Genitourinary: Unremarkable

Musculoskeletal: Unremarkable

Neurologic: Unremarkable

Mental status: Unremarkable

Vignette:
A 72-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history and known COPD (GOLD stage II) presents with a 5-day history of increased sputum production and mild worsening of his baseline dyspnea. He reports his sputum has changed from white to yellow-green. He denies fever, chest pain, hemoptysis, or significant increase in cough frequency. He is currently using tiotropium and an albuterol rescue inhaler as needed. Vital signs show temperature 98.6°F, heart rate 82, blood pressure 134/78, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 93% on room air (baseline 94-95%). On examination, there is mild bilateral expiratory wheezing without accessory muscle use. He is speaking in full sentences comfortably.

Vignette:
A 72-year-old woman presents with generalized dry, itchy skin that has been worsening over the past several weeks as winter has progressed. She reports the itching is worst on her shins and forearms. She bathes daily in hot water and uses regular bar soap. She denies any new medications, rash, jaundice, or unintentional weight loss. On examination, the skin on the extremities is diffusely dry with fine scaling and superficial cracking. There are no excoriations, erythematous plaques, or papules. Skin turgor is appropriate for age. No jaundice or lymphadenopathy is noted.

Vignette:
A 20-year-old female college student who recently started a running program presents with bilateral dull, aching pain along the front of both shins. The pain began about 1 week ago and occurs primarily during and shortly after running, then resolves with rest. She runs on paved surfaces in her current athletic shoes that are over a year old. She denies pain at rest, nighttime pain, swelling, or history of stress fractures. On examination, there is mild tenderness on palpation along the medial border of the bilateral tibias spanning approximately 5 cm. There is no point tenderness, edema, or erythema. Ankle range of motion and strength are normal.

Vignette:
A 17-year-old female is brought in by her parents after they discovered an empty bottle of extra-strength acetaminophen (500 mg tablets, 50-count) in her room. She admits to intentionally ingesting approximately 25 grams 12 hours ago following a breakup. She initially felt fine but now reports nausea, vomiting, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. On examination, she is tearful but cooperative. Vital signs: T 37.2C, HR 96, RR 18, BP 112/68, SpO2 99%. Abdomen is tender in the right upper quadrant. Scleral icterus is not yet present. Labs: acetaminophen level 180 mcg/mL (well above treatment line on Rumack-Matthew nomogram at 12 hours), AST 1,240 U/L, ALT 1,086 U/L, INR 1.8, total bilirubin 2.1 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, pH 7.34, lactate 2.8 mmol/L. N-acetylcysteine infusion is initiated immediately. Psychiatry and social work consultations are placed. Poison control is contacted.

Vignette:
A 70-year-old man presents with 18 hours of worsening right upper quadrant pain, fever with rigors, and progressive yellowing of his skin and eyes. He has a history of choledocholithiasis with a prior ERCP and sphincterotomy 5 years ago. On examination, he appears jaundiced and acutely ill with intermittent rigors. Vital signs: T 39.6C, HR 118, RR 22, BP 88/52, SpO2 96%. Abdominal examination reveals significant right upper quadrant tenderness with a positive Murphy sign. Scleral icterus is prominent. Labs: WBC 22,600/mcL with 15% bands, total bilirubin 8.4 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 6.8 mg/dL, ALP 482 U/L, AST 188 U/L, ALT 162 U/L, lipase normal, lactate 4.1 mmol/L. Blood cultures are drawn. Right upper quadrant ultrasound shows common bile duct dilation to 14 mm with a shadowing stone in the distal CBD and mild intrahepatic ductal dilation.

Vignette:
A 3-year-old girl is brought in by her mother with a low-grade fever of 37.8°C and small blisters noticed on her hands and feet since this morning. The mother also notes a few small sores inside the child's mouth. The child is eating and drinking well, though slightly fussier than usual. Several children at her daycare have had similar symptoms. On examination, there are scattered small vesicles on the palms, soles, and a few on the dorsal hands. Two shallow ulcers are seen on the buccal mucosa. The child is alert, playful, and well-hydrated.

Vignette:
A 68-yr-old woman comes to the office with her daughter because of a 4-mo history of gradually
increasing lethargy and worsening memory. Her daughter is concerned because the mother has
stopped remembering whether she has taken her regular medications. The daughter is worried
that her mother might not be safe to live on her own. Prior to 4 mo ago, the woman had been
very busy with community activities, which she has since stopped, and her daughter had not
noticed any memory difficulties. The daughter is not aware of any recent illnesses or injuries.

Review of Systems:
General: The patient says she feels tired all the time and is usually cold even now during the
summer. She has a poor appetite but has gained 5 kg in weight in the preceding 4 mo despite
decreased appetite. No fever, chills, headache, or body aches.

Skin: Her skin has become dry, and her hair is now coarse and sparse. No rash or itching.

HEENT: She reports fullness in her throat, and her daughter has noticed that her mother's
voice has become hoarse and her face appears puffy, particularly around the eyes. No difficulty
swallowing.

Pulmonary: The patient reports new exertional shortness of breath and needing to pause after
climbing 1/2 flight of stairs. No cough or wheezing.

Cardiovascular: She used to have occasional palpitations before but has had none for the last 2
mo. She denies chest pain, orthopnea, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.

Gastrointestinal: The patient's bowel movements have decreased from daily to once every 3
to 4 days when using laxatives. She does not have any abdominal pain or vomiting. Her
appetite is decreased.

Genitourinary: Noncontributory

Musculoskeletal: Her ankles and lower legs are more swollen than they used to be. She reports
fatigue and leg weakness when climbing stairs or getting up from a chair.

Neurologic: She has become slower at performing daily activities, and extra effort is required.
Her daughter has noticed that her mother has trouble remembering recent events, such as
whether she has taken her medications. She denies having focal weakness or sensory
abnormalities, tremor, or visual symptoms.

Psychiatric: Her mood is depressed and she often stays in bed, not going out of the house for
many days.

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Hypertension diagnosed 10 yr ago and controlled with three antihypertensives.
Atrial fibrillation (AF) rate-controlled with bisoprolol; previous admission to hospital with a fast
AF complicated with acute left ventricular failure; cardioversion failed to restore sinus rhythm.

Surgical history: Appendectomy at the age of 19 yr, left carpal tunnel syndrome surgery 2 yr
ago.

Medications: Bisoprolol 5 mg once/day, ramipril 10 mg once/day, furosemide 40 mg once/day,
warfarin 3 mg once/day.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Family history: Mother had hypothyroidism and a stroke in her 80s. Father died of metastatic
colon cancer.

Social history: She eats a healthy balanced diet, and her only exercise is walking to nearby
shops twice a week. She used to work as a receptionist but retired 3 yr ago. She is a
nonsmoker and drinks alcohol only occasionally. She has not travelled abroad in the last 3 yr.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: The patient is wearing several layers of clothing including a wool sweater
despite it being 89° F outside. She has a dull facial expression, and she looks pale and tired.

Vital signs:

Temperature: 35.8° C
Pulse: 56 beats/min, irregular
BP: 120/90 mm Hg
Respirations: 16/min

Skin: Skin is cool and dry, no cyanosis or rash. Hair is coarse and dry with noticeable loss of
hair from the eyebrows.

HEENT: Periorbital edema. Thyroid gland is slightly enlarged bilaterally, firm, and nontender.
There is no cervical lymphadenopathy.

Pulmonary: Good air entry and exit with a few bibasilar fine end-inspiratory crackles and no
wheeze.

Cardiovascular: Irregularly irregular heart rate of 56 beats/min, no murmurs, rubs or gallops.
Jugular venous pulse visible but not elevated. There is 2+ edema of both lower extremities.
Dorsalis pedis pulses are difficult to palpate due to leg edema.

Gastrointestinal: Previous appendectomy scar is visible. Abdomen is soft; there is a mild
discomfort in the left iliac fossa with normal bowel sounds. Hard, brown, stool is present in the
rectum on the rectal examination. Stool is negative for occult blood.

Genitourinary: Unremarkable

Musculoskeletal: A left wrist scar is present from surgical decompression of carpal tunnel
syndrome. Tinel's sign is positive on the right side.

Neurologic: Patient 's movements and speech are slow but clear, no tremor. Cranial nerves
II-XII intact. There is proximal weakness (4+/5) of both lower extremities, otherwise strength and
muscle tone are normal and symmetrical; deep tendon reflexes are decreased generally with a
prolonged relaxation phase. Plantar reflexes are down-going bilaterally.

Mental status: Patient reports a decreased mood but no suicidal thoughts.

Test Results:

Platelets 159,000/mcL
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) 88 fL
Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC) 34 g/dL
Chest x-ray: Small volume fluid in the right interlobar fissure, mild bibasilar atelectasis, enlarged
heart size.
Head CT: Normal

Results of ECG are shown.

Vignette:
Mrs. L is a 61 year-old woman who presents with 4 days of a cough productive of yellow sputum. Her symptoms started 4 days ago with rhinorrhea and productive cough. She initially had fevers as high as 101 for 2 days, but those have now resolved. In the office, she has normal vital signs and a normal physical examination. She is otherwise healthy except for high cholesterol for which she is being treated with atorvastatin. She has no drug allergies.

Vignette:
A 9-month-old male infant is brought in by his parents after 8 hours of episodic inconsolable crying during which he draws his legs up to his abdomen, alternating with periods of lethargy. The parents report two episodes of vomiting and one bowel movement containing dark red mucus-like material. He had a viral upper respiratory infection last week. On examination, during a pain-free interval, the infant is pale and lethargic. Vital signs: T 37.4C, HR 168, RR 36, BP 80/52. Abdomen is mildly distended with a palpable sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant. The right lower quadrant feels empty (Dance sign). Rectal exam reveals currant jelly stool on the examining finger. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates a target sign (doughnut sign) in the right upper quadrant, confirming ileocolic intussusception, with no evidence of perforation or peritonitis. Air enema reduction is arranged.

Vignette:
A 70-year-old man with a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia presents to his primary care physician with a 3-day history of dysuria, urinary frequency, and urgency. He reports mild suprapubic discomfort and low-grade fever of 100.4°F. He denies flank pain, rigors, or hematuria. His past medical history is notable for BPH managed with tamsulosin. On examination, he appears mildly uncomfortable but is in no acute distress. Vital signs show temperature 100.4°F, blood pressure 138/82, heart rate 78. Abdominal examination reveals mild suprapubic tenderness without guarding. Digital rectal exam shows an enlarged, nontender prostate. Urinalysis demonstrates pyuria and positive nitrites.

Vignette:
A 66-year-old woman presents with 2 days of progressive abdominal distension, diffuse crampy abdominal pain, and intractable vomiting that has become bilious and feculent. She has not passed flatus or had a bowel movement for 36 hours. Her surgical history includes an open appendectomy 30 years ago and a total abdominal hysterectomy 15 years ago. On examination, she appears dehydrated and in moderate distress. Vital signs: T 37.8C, HR 110, RR 20, BP 108/68, SpO2 97%. Abdomen is markedly distended and tympanitic with high-pitched tinkling bowel sounds. There is diffuse tenderness, greatest in the periumbilical region, with mild involuntary guarding. Labs: WBC 14,800/mcL, BUN 42, creatinine 1.6, lactate 3.1 mmol/L. CT abdomen demonstrates dilated small bowel loops up to 5.2 cm with a discrete transition point in the right lower quadrant with a small bowel feces sign and possible closed-loop configuration.

Vignette:
A 40-year-old male construction worker is extricated by rescue crews after being trapped under a collapsed concrete wall at a building site for approximately 4 hours. Both lower extremities were pinned. Upon extrication, he is alert and reports severe pain in both legs and a sensation of numbness. He has no significant past medical history. On examination, both lower extremities are markedly swollen, tense, and ecchymotic from the thighs to the ankles. Vital signs: T 36.4C, HR 118, RR 24, BP 96/62, SpO2 95%. Pedal pulses are weak bilaterally. Sensation is diminished throughout both legs. He reports dark brown urine since a Foley catheter was placed in the field, with only 50 mL output over the past 2 hours. Labs drawn immediately: potassium 6.8 mEq/L, creatinine 3.4 mg/dL, CK 124,000 U/L, phosphorus 7.6 mg/dL, calcium 6.2 mg/dL, uric acid 14.2 mg/dL, myoglobin 48,000 ng/mL, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, lactate 6.8 mmol/L. ECG shows peaked T waves. Aggressive IV normal saline resuscitation at 1.5 L/hr with sodium bicarbonate supplementation is initiated, along with continuous cardiac monitoring and IV calcium gluconate for cardioprotection.

Vignette:
A 47-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of the worst headache of her life that began 1 hour ago while straining during a bowel movement. She describes it as a thunderclap headache reaching maximum intensity within seconds. She experienced one episode of vomiting and brief loss of consciousness. Her past medical history includes migraines and she is a current smoker. On examination, she is photophobic, irritable, and has a stiff neck. Vital signs: T 37.4C, HR 96, RR 18, BP 178/96, SpO2 98%. Neurological exam reveals intact cranial nerves, mild bilateral lower extremity weakness, and pronounced nuchal rigidity. Hunt and Hess grade III. Non-contrast CT head reveals diffuse subarachnoid hemorrhage in the basal cisterns. CT angiography identifies a 7 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm.

Vignette:
A 5-month-old baby boy presents with difficulty and delay in passing hard stools. His mother reports that he strains for several hours and may even miss a day, before passing stool with screaming and occasional spots of fresh blood on the stool or diaper. He has recently been weaned from breastfeeding to cows' milk formula, which he had been reluctant to drink initially. The child is thriving and now feeding normally. There was no neonatal delay in defecation and no history of excessive vomiting or abdominal distension.

Vignette:
A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency department with acute onset of SOB of 30 minutes' duration. Initially, he felt faint but did not lose consciousness. He is complaining of left-sided chest pain that worsens on deep inspiration. He has no history of cardiopulmonary disease. A week ago he underwent a total left hip replacement and, following discharge, was on bed rest for 3 days due to poorly controlled pain. He subsequently noticed swelling in his left calf, which is tender on examination. His current vital signs reveal a fever of 100.4°F (38.0°C), heart rate 112 bpm, BP 95/65, and an O2 saturation on room air of 91%.

Vignette:
A 32-year-old woman at 34 weeks gestation (G3P2) presents with sudden onset of painful vaginal bleeding and severe constant abdominal pain that began 30 minutes ago. She has a history of chronic hypertension managed with labetalol and a prior placental abruption with her second pregnancy. She reports the baby's movements have decreased since the bleeding started. On examination, she is anxious, pale, and in significant distress. Vital signs: T 36.8C, HR 124, RR 24, BP 96/62, SpO2 96%. The uterus is firm, tender, and contracted (woody consistency) with no relaxation between contractions. Moderate dark red vaginal bleeding is present. Continuous fetal monitoring reveals a baseline fetal heart rate of 170 bpm with absent variability and repetitive late decelerations. Labs: hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL, platelets 108,000/mcL, fibrinogen 142 mg/dL (low), PT 14.8 seconds, D-dimer >20,000 ng/mL. Transfusion is initiated and emergent cesarean delivery is called.

Vignette:
A 30-year-old man presents to the urgent care clinic with a 6-hour history of severe pain, tearing, and foreign body sensation in his left eye. He was grinding metal at work without wearing safety goggles when he felt something strike his eye. Since then, he has had constant sharp pain, profuse tearing, photophobia, and difficulty keeping the eye open. He denies any change in vision other than blurriness from tearing. He wears contact lenses but removed them immediately after the incident. On examination, visual acuity is 20/30 in the left eye (baseline 20/20) and 20/20 in the right. There is conjunctival injection of the left eye with no hypopyon or hyphema. The pupil is round and reactive. Fluorescein staining under cobalt blue light reveals a 3 mm linear epithelial defect on the central cornea. Seidel test is negative. There is no retained foreign body visible on slit lamp examination or eversion of the upper lid.

Vignette:
A 68-year-old man presents with sudden onset of severe pain, coldness, and numbness in his left leg that started approximately 3 hours ago while sitting at home. He has a history of atrial fibrillation and was recently taken off warfarin due to a GI bleed. On examination, the left leg is pale and cool to the touch from the mid-thigh distally. Vital signs: T 36.9C, HR 88 (irregularly irregular), RR 16, BP 148/86, SpO2 97%. Left dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are absent by palpation and Doppler. Left popliteal pulse is faintly detectable. The left calf is tender with decreased sensation and the patient is unable to dorsiflex or plantarflex the left foot. Right leg pulses are palpable and symmetric. CT angiography shows abrupt occlusion of the left superficial femoral artery.

Vignette:
An 8-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after pulling a pot of boiling water off the stove onto himself approximately 45 minutes ago. He sustained scald burns to his anterior chest, abdomen, both upper extremities, and portions of his face. He has been crying inconsolably. He has no significant past medical history. On examination, he is alert but in severe pain and distress. Vital signs: T 36.6C, HR 152, RR 28, BP 94/58, SpO2 98%. Weight is 28 kg. Burns cover approximately 20% total body surface area: areas of erythema with large intact and ruptured blisters (superficial partial thickness) on the chest and abdomen, with waxy white insensate areas (deep partial to full thickness) on both forearms. No circumferential burns are identified. Facial burns are superficial with no singed nasal hairs and no evidence of inhalation injury. He has no hoarseness or stridor. Parkland formula is calculated (20% TBSA x 28 kg x 4 mL = 2,240 mL LR over first 24 hours), IV access is obtained, and morphine is administered for pain.

Vignette:
A 29-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician reporting 8 months of near-constant excessive worry about multiple domains of her life including work performance, finances, health, and her children's safety. She describes an inability to control the worry despite recognizing it is disproportionate. She reports associated restlessness, muscle tension predominantly in her neck and shoulders, difficulty falling asleep, irritability, and difficulty concentrating during meetings. She has tried meditation and exercise with only partial benefit. She denies panic attacks, specific phobias, obsessive thoughts, or traumatic experiences. She has no prior psychiatric history and takes no medications. She drinks one cup of coffee daily. Vital signs are normal. Physical examination reveals bilateral trapezius muscle tightness but is otherwise unremarkable. Thyroid function tests are within normal limits. GAD-7 score is 16 indicating severe anxiety.

Vignette:
A 40-year-old woman presents with a 2-year history of persistent nasal congestion, frequent sneezing, and clear rhinorrhea. She notes that symptoms are present year-round but worsen when she vacuums or dusts her home. She denies any history of asthma, wheezing, or shortness of breath. She has tried over-the-counter antihistamines intermittently with partial relief. On examination, nasal mucosa is pale and boggy bilaterally. There is a transverse nasal crease. No nasal polyps are visualized. Lungs are clear to auscultation. She lives in an older home with carpeted bedrooms and reports no pets.

Vignette:
A 16-year-old female high school student presents with complaints of fever, sore throat, and fatigue. She started feeling sick 1 week ago. Her symptoms are gradually getting worse, and she has difficulty swallowing. She has had a fever every day, and she could hardly get out of bed this morning. She does not remember being exposed to anybody with a similar illness recently. On physical examination she is febrile and looks sick. Enlarged cervical lymph nodes, exudative pharyngitis with soft palate petechiae and faint erythematous macular rash on the trunk and arms are found.

Vignette:
A 4-year-old boy is brought in by his parents after 6 hours of rapidly progressive sore throat, difficulty swallowing, and noisy breathing. He has had no significant past medical history and immunizations are not up to date (parents declined some vaccines). On examination, the child is sitting upright in a tripod position, leaning forward with his neck extended and jaw thrust forward. He is drooling profusely and appears anxious and toxic-appearing. Vital signs: T 39.8C, HR 162, RR 34, SpO2 92% on room air. Inspiratory stridor is audible without a stethoscope. His voice is muffled and he refuses to speak or drink. A soft tissue lateral neck X-ray obtained reveals a thumb sign consistent with epiglottic swelling. Anesthesiology and ENT are urgently called for airway management.

Vignette:
A 35-year-old man is referred by his primary care physician for psychiatric evaluation after presenting with a 2-month history of persistent low mood, loss of interest in activities he previously enjoyed including playing guitar and socializing, insomnia with early morning awakening, decreased appetite with an unintentional 14-pound weight loss, difficulty concentrating at work, and pervasive feelings of worthlessness. He describes his mood as an overwhelming heaviness that does not lift. He has been increasingly isolating from friends and family. He denies suicidal ideation, hallucinations, or delusions. He has no prior psychiatric history. He went through a significant relationship breakup 3 months ago. Vital signs are normal. On mental status examination, he is casually dressed with poor grooming. Psychomotor retardation is present. Speech is soft and slow. Affect is flat. Thought process is linear but impoverished. PHQ-9 score is 22 indicating severe depression.

Vignette:
A 72-year-old man presents with 3 days of vague periumbilical discomfort that has gradually localized to the right lower quadrant. He reports decreased appetite, mild nausea, and one episode of loose stool. His past medical history includes type 2 diabetes, coronary artery disease, and a total knee replacement. On examination, he is afebrile at 37.2C but appears mildly uncomfortable. Vital signs: HR 92, RR 18, BP 134/78, SpO2 97%. Abdominal exam reveals mild right lower quadrant tenderness without guarding or rebound. WBC is only mildly elevated at 11,200/mcL. CT abdomen with contrast shows a dilated appendix measuring 14 mm with periappendiceal fat stranding and a small contained fluid collection suggestive of early perforation.

Vignette:
A 29-year-old male software developer presents with eye fatigue, dryness, and a mild headache that worsens throughout the workday. He spends 10 to 12 hours daily in front of computer screens and often forgets to take breaks. He reports that symptoms improve on weekends when he reduces screen time. He denies blurred vision, floaters, flashes of light, or eye pain. He does not wear corrective lenses. On examination, visual acuity is 20/20 bilaterally. Extraocular movements are intact. Pupils are equal and reactive. Conjunctivae are mildly injected. The anterior segment and fundoscopic exams are normal bilaterally.

Vignette:
A 56-year-old woman with a history of smoking presents to her primary care physician with shortness of breath and cough for several days. Her symptoms began 3 days ago with rhinorrhea. She reports a chronic morning cough productive of white sputum, which has increased over the past 2 days. She has had similar episodes each winter for the past 4 years. She has smoked 1 to 2 packs of cigarettes per day for 40 years and continues to smoke. She denies hemoptysis, chills, or weight loss and has not received any relief from over-the-counter cough preparations.

Vignette:
A 25-year-old woman presents with 3 days of clear nasal discharge, mild sore throat, and occasional sneezing. She works as a daycare teacher and reports several children in her class have had similar symptoms. She denies fever, cough, dyspnea, ear pain, or facial pressure. On examination, temperature is 37.0°C. The oropharynx shows mild erythema without exudates. Nasal mucosa is mildly edematous with clear discharge. Tympanic membranes are normal bilaterally. Cervical lymph nodes are not enlarged. She is well-appearing and in no distress.

Vignette:
A 5-year-old boy is brought in by his mother who noticed multiple itchy red bumps on his arms and legs after he spent the afternoon playing outside in the backyard. The bumps appeared over the past 24 hours. He has been scratching but the mother reports no significant swelling beyond the immediate area of each bump. He denies fever, joint pain, or any recent travel. On examination, there are approximately 8 to 10 small erythematous papules, each 3 to 5 mm in diameter, scattered on the bilateral forearms and lower legs. Several have small central puncta. There is no surrounding cellulitis, lymphangitis, or regional lymphadenopathy.

Vignette:
A 24-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of dysuria and urinary frequency that has progressed to right flank pain, fever, and rigors over the past 24 hours. She reports nausea and one episode of vomiting. She has had two previous urinary tract infections in the past year treated with antibiotics. She is sexually active and uses oral contraceptives. She denies vaginal discharge or hematuria. Vital signs show temperature 102.2°F, heart rate 104, blood pressure 108/66, respiratory rate 18. On examination, she appears flushed and mildly uncomfortable. There is significant right costovertebral angle tenderness on percussion. Abdominal exam reveals mild suprapubic tenderness without guarding. Urinalysis shows large leukocyte esterase, positive nitrites, many white blood cells, and bacteria. A point-of-care pregnancy test is negative.

Vignette:
A 77-year-old man reports a 5-day history of burning and aching pain on the right side of his chest. This is followed by the development of erythema and a maculopapular rash in this painful area, accompanied by headache and malaise. The rash progressed to develop clusters of clear vesicles for 3 to 5 days, evolving through stages of pustulation, ulceration, and crusting.

Vignette:
A 28-year-old woman with known epilepsy is brought in by ambulance after her roommate witnessed continuous generalized tonic-clonic seizure activity for approximately 12 minutes. EMS administered 10 mg of intramuscular midazolam en route, but seizure activity persisted. Her past medical history includes focal epilepsy diagnosed at age 16, treated with levetiracetam. Her roommate reports she recently missed several doses of medication due to insurance issues. On arrival, she remains in continuous generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Vital signs: T 39.2C, HR 142, RR (irregular, 8-30), BP 168/98, SpO2 88% on non-rebreather mask. She is cyanotic around the lips. Finger-stick glucose is 142 mg/dL. IV lorazepam 4 mg is administered with brief cessation of convulsive activity, but seizures resume within 2 minutes.

Vignette:
A 31-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 6-month history of nipple discharge. She
has noticed that her breasts are tender and both nipples produce milky discharge on applying
mild pressure. She has not noted any bloody or clear nipple discharge, breast lumps, or skin
changes. She also states she has not had a menstrual period for 6 months, and her periods had
been irregular for 8 months before they stopped altogether. Prior to her menstrual irregularities,
her menses occurred at a normal frequency and duration. She is sexually active with a single
partner and is trying to conceive.

Review of Systems:
General: Gradually increasing lethargy over the past 2 months. 3 kg unintentional weight gain in
the past 6 months.

Skin: No rash or history of excessive facial hair or acne.

HEENT: No rhinorrhea, tinnitus, vertigo, or change in hearing.

Pulmonary: Noncontributory

Cardiovascular: Noncontributory

Gastrointestinal: Noncontributory

Genitourinary: Noncontributory

Gynecologic: Decreased libido. Vaginal dryness during sexual intercourse. She has been trying
to conceive for the last 2 years. One full-term, uncomplicated pregnancy 5 years ago.

Musculoskeletal: Noncontributory

Neurologic: 6-month history of dull frontal and occasionally retro-orbital headaches that are
increasing in frequency and that now occur almost daily and affect her work performance. There
are no associated neurologic symptoms, including disturbances of vision, strength, balance, or
gait. She denies nausea, photophobia, or phonophobia. Until 1 month ago, the headaches
would resolve completely with nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs, but for the last month taking
simple analgesia does not suffice. She denies history of headaches prior to 6 months ago.

Psychiatric: She is mildly depressed recently, which she attributes to the frequent headaches.
No suicidal ideation.

Past Medical History:
Medical history: She had mild asthma in childhood, which she outgrew. She has a 5-year-old
son after an uncomplicated pregnancy with spontaneous vertex delivery at 40 weeks.

Surgical history: No previous operations.

Medications: Acetaminophen 1 g daily as needed; ibuprofen 400 mg daily as needed. Ibuprofen
recently increased to as much as 400 to 600 mg twice daily.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Family history: Her father had a stroke in his 80s; mother had osteoporosis.

Social history: She eats a healthy balanced diet. She does not exercise regularly. She is
nonsmoker and drinks alcohol very occasionally. She works as a primary school teacher. Her
last travel outside the country was to Italy 8 months ago.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: Comfortable-appearing female who generally looks well and appears her
stated age.

Vital signs:
BMI: 22 kg/m2
Temperature: 36.6° C
Pulse: 80 beats/minute and regular
Respirations: 18/min
BP: 135/74 mm Hg

Skin: Normal color, no rash, hirsutism, or acne.

HEENT: Pupils equal and reactive to light and accommodation. Normal visual fields to
confrontation. Visual acuity 20/20 in both eyes. Fundi normal bilaterally. No thyroid enlargement

Pulmonary: Equal air entry and chest is clear on auscultation. No crackles or wheezes.

Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm with normal heart sounds. No murmurs. Normal

GYN: No breast masses or skin changes. No axillary lymphadenopathy. Mild diffuse breast
