Vignette:
A 38-year-old woman presents with a 3-week history of persistent throat clearing and a mild cough that is worse when lying down at night. She reports a sensation of mucus dripping in the back of her throat. She recently had a mild cold that resolved 4 weeks ago. She denies fever, facial pain, purulent nasal discharge, wheezing, or heartburn. She is a non-smoker. On examination, the oropharynx shows a cobblestone appearance of the posterior pharyngeal wall. Nasal mucosa is mildly erythematous with clear thin secretions. Lungs are clear to auscultation. There is no sinus tenderness on palpation.

Vignette:
A 19-year-old tall, thin male (6'3", 145 lbs) presents with sudden onset of sharp right-sided pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea that began 2 hours ago while playing basketball. He has no prior medical history, takes no medications, and does not smoke. On examination, he is mildly tachypneic but speaking in full sentences. Vital signs: T 36.8C, HR 104, RR 22, BP 128/76, SpO2 93% on room air. The right hemithorax is hyperresonant to percussion with decreased breath sounds on the right compared to the left. Chest X-ray reveals a large right-sided pneumothorax with approximately 60% lung collapse and no mediastinal shift. There is no evidence of pleural effusion.

Vignette:
A 50-year-old woman presents with a 5-day history of persistent dizziness described as a sensation of spinning. She reports the dizziness is constant rather than positional and is accompanied by an unsteady gait and difficulty walking in a straight line. She has had two episodes of nausea and vomiting. She denies hearing loss or tinnitus. Past medical history is notable for migraine headaches and hypertension. On examination, vital signs are stable. Neurological exam reveals vertical nystagmus that does not suppress with fixation, mild dysmetria on finger-to-nose testing on the right, and gait ataxia with veering to the right. Hearing is intact bilaterally. Dix-Hallpike maneuver is negative.

Vignette:
Mr. A is a 24 year-old man who presents to your office for complaints of sore throat, fever, and headache. His symptoms started 2 days ago with acute onset of sore throat and fever to 102.2. He has had no cough. His physical examination is normal, except for the presence of tonsillar exudates and some tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy. He is otherwise in good health, and is on no medications except for ibuprofen for fever. He has no drug allergies. (, Centor score = 4 – treat, or test and treat)

Vignette:
A 19-year-old man presents with a 5-day history of severe sore throat that has progressively worsened despite 3 days of oral amoxicillin prescribed for pharyngitis. He now reports difficulty swallowing and has been unable to eat solid food for 2 days. He describes a muffled "hot potato" voice and difficulty fully opening his mouth. He has been drooling due to pain with swallowing. He denies respiratory difficulty. Vital signs show temperature 101.4°F, heart rate 98, blood pressure 124/78. On examination, there is trismus with limited mouth opening to approximately 2 cm. Intraoral exam reveals a bulging, erythematous soft palate on the left with displacement of the left tonsil medially and inferiorly. The uvula is deviated to the right. There is tender left anterior cervical and submandibular lymphadenopathy. Lung auscultation is clear and there is no stridor.

Vignette:
A 30-year-old man presents with a 1-week history of mildly itchy, erythematous patches on both hands. He recently switched to a new laundry detergent approximately two weeks ago. He denies any history of atopic dermatitis, asthma, or food allergies. On examination, there are bilateral, symmetric, well-demarcated erythematous plaques on the dorsal hands with mild scaling. The skin is intact with no cracking, vesicles, or weeping. There is no involvement of the wrists or forearms. He works as an accountant and reports no occupational chemical exposures.

Vignette:
A 28-year-old woman presents with a 1-day history of nausea, three episodes of watery non-bloody diarrhea, and mild diffuse abdominal cramping. She reports her roommate had similar symptoms earlier in the week. She is able to tolerate oral fluids and has been sipping water and electrolyte drinks throughout the day. She denies fever, bloody stool, severe abdominal pain, or dizziness. On examination, vital signs are stable. The abdomen is soft with mild diffuse tenderness, no guarding or rebound. Mucous membranes are moist. Bowel sounds are hyperactive.

Vignette:
A 60-year-old woman presents with 5 days of progressive shortness of breath following a confirmed influenza A infection. Despite oseltamivir initiated 3 days ago, her respiratory status has continued to deteriorate. She has a history of well-controlled type 2 diabetes and obesity (BMI 38). On examination, she is in marked respiratory distress. Vital signs: T 38.9C, HR 118, RR 34, BP 106/62, SpO2 82% on high-flow nasal cannula at 60L/min and FiO2 100%. Lung auscultation reveals diffuse bilateral crackles. Chest X-ray demonstrates bilateral diffuse alveolar opacities consistent with pulmonary edema, but echocardiogram shows normal left ventricular function with no evidence of volume overload. ABG: pH 7.22, pO2 58, pCO2 52, PaO2/FiO2 ratio 58. She is intubated for mechanical ventilation.

Vignette:
A 32-year-old woman who is 4 months postpartum presents with a 6-week history of pain along the radial (thumb) side of her right wrist. The pain began insidiously and has progressively worsened. She attributes it to the repetitive motions of lifting and holding her infant. The pain is sharp and radiates proximally into the forearm and distally into the thumb. She reports difficulty gripping objects, turning her wrist, and making a fist. She is right-hand dominant. On examination, there is tenderness and mild swelling over the radial styloid process and the first dorsal compartment. Finkelstein test is markedly positive, reproducing sharp pain along the radial wrist when the thumb is grasped in a fist and the wrist is ulnarly deviated. Grip strength is reduced due to pain. Thumb range of motion is preserved but painful at extremes. Neurovascular examination of the hand is intact. Wrist radiographs are normal.

Vignette:
A 62-year-old man with chronic kidney disease stage 4 (baseline GFR 22) on maintenance hemodialysis presents after missing his last two dialysis sessions due to transportation issues. He reports 2 days of progressive generalized weakness, muscle cramps, and palpitations. He has continued to eat his usual diet, including bananas and orange juice. On examination, he appears fatigued and mildly short of breath. Vital signs: T 36.6C, HR 52 (irregular), RR 20, BP 172/96, SpO2 95%. Lower extremity exam reveals 2+ bilateral pitting edema and diminished deep tendon reflexes. Labs: potassium 7.8 mEq/L, BUN 112 mg/dL, creatinine 11.4 mg/dL, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, phosphorus 8.2 mg/dL. ECG demonstrates absent P waves, widened QRS complexes (duration 180 ms), and peaked T waves with a sine wave pattern beginning to emerge. IV calcium gluconate is administered emergently.

Vignette:
A 15-year-old girl presents with her mother for evaluation of bumps on her forehead and chin that have been present for the past 3 months. She reports they are not painful but she finds them cosmetically bothersome. She has been washing her face with regular soap twice daily. She denies any cystic lesions, scarring, or use of new cosmetics. Menarche was 1 year ago and her cycles are regular. She takes no medications. On examination, there are scattered open and closed comedones on the forehead and chin numbering approximately 15 to 20. A few small inflammatory papules, each less than 5 mm, are noted on the chin. There are no nodules, cysts, or scarring.

Vignette:
A 52-year-old obese man with a BMI of 36 presents for evaluation after his wife noticed he has been drinking large amounts of water and urinating frequently over the past several weeks. He reports increased thirst, frequent nighttime urination disrupting sleep, and a 10-pound unintentional weight loss over 2 months. He also describes blurry vision and increased fatigue. His past medical history includes hypertension treated with lisinopril and hyperlipidemia. Family history is significant for type 2 diabetes in both parents. He works a sedentary desk job and does not exercise regularly. Vital signs show blood pressure 144/92, heart rate 78. On examination, he is obese with acanthosis nigricans on the posterior neck and axillae. Foot examination shows intact sensation to monofilament and palpable pedal pulses. Fasting plasma glucose is 210 mg/dL, and HbA1c is 9.2%. Urinalysis shows glucosuria without ketonuria.

Vignette:
A 52-year-old woman with a 10-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with a 3-month history of progressively worsening stiffness and pain in her left shoulder. The pain is deep and aching, worse at night, and has made it increasingly difficult to reach behind her back, comb her hair, and fasten her bra. She denies any preceding trauma or injury. Her diabetes is managed with metformin and her last HbA1c was 7.8%. On examination, there is globally restricted active and passive range of motion of the left shoulder. External rotation is limited to 20 degrees (compared to 70 degrees on the right). Abduction is limited to 80 degrees, and internal rotation is severely restricted. There is no tenderness over specific rotator cuff tendons. Strength testing is limited by pain and stiffness. Shoulder radiographs show no fracture or dislocation and mild osteopenia.

Vignette:
A 40-year-old man with a known history of chronic rhinosinusitis and bilateral nasal polyps presents with a 10-day history of worsening facial pressure, purulent nasal discharge, nasal congestion, and anosmia. He has had recurrent sinus infections averaging four to five times per year and has previously undergone polypectomy two years ago. He reports postnasal drip and a productive cough worse at night. He denies fever, visual changes, or severe headache. On examination, the nasal mucosa is edematous and erythematous bilaterally with visible polypoid tissue and mucopurulent drainage in the middle meatus. There is tenderness over the maxillary and frontal sinuses. Oropharynx shows cobblestoning of the posterior pharyngeal wall.

Vignette:
A 35-year-old male teacher presents with 2 days of nasal congestion, frequent sneezing, mild sore throat, and a low-grade temperature of 37.6°C. He reports several students in his classroom have been out sick recently. He notes mild fatigue but denies cough, dyspnea, myalgias, or ear pain. On examination, the nasal turbinates are mildly swollen with clear discharge. The oropharynx is mildly erythematous without tonsillar enlargement or exudates. Tympanic membranes are clear. Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. He is well-hydrated and in no acute distress.

Vignette:
A 35-year-old man presents with 3 days of progressive bilateral submandibular and sublingual swelling, worsening trismus, odynophagia, and a muffled "hot potato" voice. Five days ago, he had a lower left second molar extracted at a dental clinic. He has no significant past medical history. On examination, he is sitting upright and drooling, appearing anxious and in respiratory distress. Vital signs: T 38.8C, HR 114, RR 24, BP 138/82, SpO2 91% on room air. There is firm, woody, bilateral submandibular swelling with erythema and warmth. The floor of the mouth is elevated and indurated, displacing the tongue posteriorly and superiorly. He is unable to fully open his mouth. Inspiratory stridor is audible. CT neck with contrast demonstrates a multiloculated fluid collection in the submandibular and sublingual spaces bilaterally with significant airway narrowing at the level of the oropharynx.

Vignette:
A 24-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks gestation is brought in by ambulance after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home lasting approximately 2 minutes. Her partner reports she has complained of a persistent headache, visual disturbances described as flashing lights, and swelling of her face and hands over the past 2 days. She did not attend her last two prenatal appointments. On examination, she is postictal, moaning, and not following commands. Vital signs: T 37.6C, HR 112, RR 22, BP 182/116, SpO2 94%. Significant periorbital and bilateral upper extremity edema is present. Deep tendon reflexes are 4+ bilaterally with sustained clonus at the ankles. Fetal heart rate monitoring shows persistent late decelerations. Labs: platelets 92,000/mcL, AST 286 U/L, ALT 312 U/L, LDH 680 U/L, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 5.2. IV magnesium sulfate is initiated and emergent cesarean delivery is planned.

Vignette:
A 16-year-old female volleyball player presents with mild right ankle pain after landing awkwardly on another player's foot during practice 2 hours ago. She was able to walk off the court on her own. She denies hearing a pop or experiencing giving way of the ankle. She has no prior history of ankle injuries. On examination, there is mild swelling over the lateral aspect of the right ankle with mild tenderness over the anterior talofibular ligament. There is no ecchymosis. She can bear weight with minimal discomfort. Anterior drawer and talar tilt tests are negative. Bony landmarks are non-tender.

Vignette:
A 34-year-old woman with no known underlying lung disease 12-day history of cough. She initially had nasal congestion and a mild sore throat, but now her symptoms are all related to a productive cough without paroxysms. She denies any sick contacts. On physical examination she is not in respiratory distress and is afebrile with normal vital signs. No signs of URI are noted. Scattered wheezes are present diffusely on lung auscultation.

Vignette:
A 24-year-old man presents with a painful small bump in his beard area that appeared 2 days after shaving. He shaves with a multi-blade razor and shaves against the grain. He denies fever, spreading redness, or drainage. He has no history of recurrent skin infections. On examination, there is a single erythematous, firm papule approximately 4 mm in diameter on the right submandibular area. Mild swelling is present around the lesion. A curled hair is visible beneath the surface of the skin. There is no fluctuance, induration, or streaking erythema.

Vignette:
A 56-year-old woman who is a long-time patient returns to the office for scheduled follow up of her type 2 diabetes and chronically elevated blood glucose. At her last visit 3 months ago, her HbA1C was 7.6%, where it had been for several visits. You recommended beginning treatment with insulin, which she refused because of her fear of needles. You then increased her dose of glimepiride from 4 mg to 8 mg once a day and advised her to more strictly follow her diet and exercise regimen, which she claims to be doing. Since the last visit, her home fingerstick glucose levels have ranged from 119 mg/dL to 263 mg/dL (6.6 to 14.6 mmol/L) and her weight on her home scale is unchanged at about 98 kg. She describes increased thirst and urination but denies blurry vision, nonhealing ulcers, or lethargy.

Per office protocol, a fingerstick glucose test on arrival today shows glucose level of 221mg/dL (12.27 mmol/L) and hemoglobin A1C 8.1%; urine dipstick is normal.

Review of Systems:
General: Increased thirst and is drinking more water. Appetite is normal and her weight at home has been unchanged for several months. She denies lethargy, fever, chills, or night sweats.

Skin: No rash, pruritus, or lesions

HEENT: No change in vision, sore throat, dysphagia

Pulmonary: No cough, shortness of breath, wheezing

Cardiovascular: No chest pain, pressure, or discomfort; no orthopnea, dyspnea on exertion, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.

Gastrointestinal: No abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea

Genitourinary: Increased urinary frequency without urgency, dysuria, or blood in urine. No vaginal discharge or itching.

Musculoskeletal: No joint or muscle pain, no sores or lesions on feet.

Neurologic: Has numbness and tingling in both feet that comes and goes throughout the day. No headache, tremor, change in gait.

Psychiatric: No mood swings, depression, or anxiety.

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and obesity

Surgical history: Cholecystectomy 5 years prior

Medications: Metformin 1000 mg twice a day, atorvastatin 80 mg once a day, glimepiride 8 mg once a day with breakfast, lisinopril 40 mg once a day, all of which she claims to be taking faithfully.

Allergies: Penicillin, which causes rash

Family history: Father died from myocardial infarction at age 89 years, mother age 88 years has type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia.

Social history: Patient works as a social worker, has never smoked cigarettes, denies any illicit drug use, drinks 1 to 2 glasses of wine with dinner every night. She rides a stationary bike about 1 to 2 days per week for 20 minutes, which she has been able to do without difficulty. She is up to date with all immunizations. Her diet consists mainly of pizza, chicken, vegetables, fruit, pasta, and diet sodas. She is married and has a 12-year-old son. She is intermittently sexually active with her husband 1 to 2 times per month. They do not use contraception as she is no longer menstruating.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: Well-appearing female in no apparent distress, height 1.65 m, weight 95.3 kg (BMI 34.9)

Vital signs:
Temperature: 37° C
Pulse: 82 min
BP: 159/88 mmHg
Respirations: 12/min

Skin: There is velvety smooth hyperpigmentation in neck folds and under arms; no other lesions or rash.

HEENT: Moist mucous membranes, no exudates, no cervical lymphadenopathy.

Pulmonary: Clear to auscultation bilaterally, no wheezes, rales, or rhonchi.

Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Jugular venous distention normal.

Gastrointestinal: Obese abdomen, soft, non-distended, normal bowel sounds, no rebound or guarding.

Genitourinary: No signs of yeast infection or other lesions. No tenderness to flank percussion.

Musculoskeletal: No peripheral edema, swelling or tenderness. Joints full range of motion and nontender.

Neurologic: Decreased sensation to light touch in feet bilaterally. Cranial nerves II to VIII grossly intact, normal gait, strength 5/5 throughout.

Mental status: Alert and oriented x3

Test Results:
Results of appropriate testing return and are shown:

Serum

HbA1C: 8.1%
Glucose: 221 mg/dL (12.27 mmol/L)
Sodium: 138 mEq/L (138 mmol/L)
Potassium: 4.1 mEq/L (4.1 mmol/L)
Creatinine: 0.7 mg/dL ( 62 µmol/L)
BUN: 23 mg/dL (8.2 mmol/L)
Lipid Panel: Results pending

Vignette:
A 28-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of severe left-sided pelvic pain and lightheadedness that began 45 minutes ago. She reports 7 weeks of amenorrhea and a positive home pregnancy test 5 days ago. She has a history of pelvic inflammatory disease and a prior left tubal ectopic pregnancy treated with methotrexate 2 years ago. On examination, she is pale, diaphoretic, and appears acutely ill. Vital signs: T 36.4C, HR 132, RR 24, BP 78/48, SpO2 97%. Abdominal exam reveals diffuse lower abdominal tenderness with peritoneal signs. Pelvic exam demonstrates cervical motion tenderness and a tender left adnexal mass. Quantitative beta-hCG is 4,200 mIU/mL. Bedside transvaginal ultrasound reveals an empty uterus, a complex left adnexal mass with ring-of-fire sign, and significant free fluid in the pelvis and Morison's pouch. Hemoglobin returns at 7.8 g/dL. O-negative blood is ordered and the OR is alerted for emergent laparotomy.

Vignette:
A 42-year-old man presents with mild low back ache that developed after spending several hours gardening yesterday. He was bending and lifting bags of soil. The pain is localized to the lower back and does not radiate to the legs. He denies numbness, tingling, weakness, or changes in bowel or bladder function. He has no history of prior back surgery or chronic back problems. On examination, there is mild paraspinal muscle tenderness in the lumbar region bilaterally. Range of motion is mildly reduced on flexion. Straight leg raise is negative bilaterally. Neurological examination of the lower extremities is normal.

Vignette:
A 35-year-old man who jogs regularly presents with a 1-week history of an itchy rash in his groin folds. He reports the itch worsens after running and sweating. He denies any genital lesions, urinary symptoms, or prior similar episodes. On examination, there are bilateral, well-demarcated erythematous plaques with slightly raised scaly borders along the inguinal creases extending to the proximal inner thighs. The scrotum is spared. There is no central clearing or satellite lesions. No inguinal lymphadenopathy is appreciated.

Vignette:
A 22-year-old female soccer player presents to the sports medicine clinic two days after sustaining a left knee injury during a game. She reports that while pivoting to change direction she felt a sudden pop in her knee followed by immediate swelling and inability to continue playing. She was unable to bear full weight and has been using crutches since. She denies any prior knee injuries. On examination, there is a moderate effusion of the left knee. Range of motion is limited by pain and swelling. The Lachman test is positive with a soft endpoint on the left, and the anterior drawer test demonstrates increased anterior tibial translation compared to the right. McMurray test is equivocal. The collateral ligaments are stable. She is neurovascularly intact distally.

Vignette:
A 6-year-old boy is brought to his pediatrician by his mother who noticed patches of hair loss on his scalp over the past 3 weeks. The patches have been gradually enlarging and the affected areas appear scaly. He attends elementary school and his mother reports several classmates have had similar issues. He denies pain but admits to mild itching. On examination, there are two well-defined round patches of alopecia on the parietal and occipital scalp, measuring approximately 3 cm and 2 cm in diameter respectively. Within the patches, the hair shafts are broken off at the surface giving a black-dot appearance. The surrounding scalp is covered with fine gray-white scale. There is mild posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. A Wood lamp examination reveals no fluorescence. KOH preparation of plucked hairs shows endothrix spores surrounding and within the hair shaft.

Vignette:
A 9-year-old boy is brought to the ER after being stung by a bee at a picnic. He is crying hysterically. After 15 minutes of calming him down, exam reveals a swollen tender upper lip but no tongue swelling, no drooling, no stridor, no rash, and no other complaints.

Vignette:
A 32-year-old woman presents with a 10-month history of recurrent episodes of abdominal cramping and altered bowel habits. She describes lower abdominal pain that is relieved with defecation, alternating between periods of diarrhea lasting several days and constipation lasting a week. Symptoms worsen during periods of work-related stress. She denies blood in her stool, nocturnal symptoms, fever, or weight loss. Family history is negative for inflammatory bowel disease or colorectal cancer. On examination, vital signs are normal. She appears anxious but in no acute distress. Abdominal examination reveals mild tenderness in the left lower quadrant with a palpable sigmoid colon on deep palpation. No masses, organomegaly, or guarding. Rectal examination is normal. Complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, C-reactive protein, and thyroid function tests are within normal limits. Stool calprotectin is negative.

Vignette:
A 55-year-old male long-haul truck driver presents with sudden onset of severe perianal pain that began yesterday while straining during a bowel movement. The pain is constant, throbbing, and rated 8 out of 10, significantly worse with sitting and defecation. He reports a palpable lump at the anal verge. He has a long history of intermittent hemorrhoidal symptoms including minor bleeding and itching, which he has managed with over-the-counter preparations. His occupation requires prolonged sitting for 10 to 12 hours daily, and he has a low-fiber diet with poor fluid intake. He denies fever, purulent drainage, or changes in bowel habits. On examination, there is a tense, bluish-purple, spherical, tender nodule approximately 2 cm in diameter at the anal verge, consistent with a thrombosed external hemorrhoid. There is surrounding mild edema but no erythema suggesting infection. Digital rectal exam is deferred due to pain.

Vignette:
A 22-year-old student presents with a 5-year history of worsening nasal congestion, sneezing, and nasal itching. Symptoms are year-round but worse during the spring season. On further questioning it is revealed that he has significant eye itching, redness, and tearing as well as palate and throat itching during the spring season. He remembers that his mother told him at some point that he used to have eczema in infancy.

Vignette:
A 30-year-old woman presents in January with 2-day history of fever, cough, headache, and generalized weakness. She was in her usual state of health before an abrupt onset of these symptoms. A few viral illnesses have affected her during the current winter, but not to this severity. She reports sick contacts at work and did not receive the seasonal influenza vaccine this season.

Vignette:
A 38-year-old male computer programmer presents with perianal discomfort and a small palpable lump that he noticed 3 days ago. He reports mild itching in the area, particularly after prolonged sitting. He denies rectal bleeding, pain during bowel movements, fever, or changes in bowel habits. He spends 8 to 10 hours daily seated at his desk. He has no family history of colorectal cancer. On examination, a small non-tender, soft, external perianal skin tag approximately 5 mm is noted at the 6 o'clock position. There is no thrombosis, bleeding, prolapse, or surrounding erythema.

Vignette:
A 58-year-old man with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh class C) presents after two episodes of large-volume hematemesis over the past hour, each estimated at 500 mL of bright red blood with clots. He also reports black tarry stools for the past 2 days. He has known esophageal varices documented on prior endoscopy and has been non-compliant with propranolol therapy. On examination, he is pale, confused, and in moderate distress. Vital signs: T 36.2C, HR 128, RR 24, BP 78/42, SpO2 94%. Abdominal exam reveals ascites, splenomegaly, and caput medusae. Rectal exam shows melena. Labs: hemoglobin 6.2 g/dL (baseline 10.4), platelets 62,000/mcL, INR 2.4, BUN 58 mg/dL. Two large-bore IVs are placed and massive transfusion protocol is activated.

Vignette:
A man who appears to be in his 50s is brought to the emergency department. The history is
given by emergency medical technicians (EMTs), who state they were called to a store for a 50-
yr-old man who possibly had a stroke. At the store, they found him lying on the ground
unconscious but breathing normally. After their arrival, the patient awoke but was unable to give
coherent responses to questions or commands.
Store employees who saw the patient reported to EMTs that he fell to the ground suddenly from
a sitting position, then began drooling, and his arms and legs shook for what seemed to be a
long time, but they cannot quantify how long. They state he had not appeared ill before the
event.

Review of Systems:
Patient is unable to provide any information at this time.

Past Medical History:
Not available at this time.

Physical Examination:
General apperance: Awake; saliva and blood at corner of his mouth. He appears well-
developed, and appearance is consistent with stated age.

Vital signs:
Temperature: 36.5° C (97.7° F)
Pulse: 80 beats/min and regular
BP: 165/90 mm Hg
Respirations: 20/min

Skin: Pink, warm, and dry, with a few punctate red spots on right lower leg

HEENT: No evidence of scalp trauma. Tympanic membranes are clear; there is a puncture
wound on the bottom of his tongue. HEENT exam is otherwise unremarkable.

Pulmonary: No respiratory distress. Equal breath sounds bilaterally with good air entry/exit; no
wheezing.

Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. Normal S1 and S2. No murmurs.

Gastrointestinal: Unremarkable

Genitourinary: Unremarkable except for urine on trousers.

Musculoskeletal: Full range of motion; no deformities, tenderness, or bruises.

Neurologic: Pupils are equal and normally reactive to light with no nystagmus. Face appears
symmetric; gag reflex is present and symmetric. The patient can move all limbs equally to
command but patient does not comprehend commands for more detailed motor function testing.
Deep tendon reflexes are symmetric and 2+ throughout; plantar reflexes are downgoing
bilaterally. No meningismus.

Mental status: Awake; eyes open. Oriented only to name; gives confused, incoherent responses
to other questions; follows simple commands using all limbs.
* Shortly after initial examination, the patient becomes extremely lethargic. He responds
to deep pain by withdrawing, and he is able to protect his airway.

He is noted to have the following: heart rate 30 beats/min, BP 74/52 mm Hg, respirations
10/min, and pulse oximetry 94% on room air. His pupils remain equal and reactive.

Test Results:
Results of appropriate studies and additional information gathering show the following:

Blood:
Test (units)
Result
Hemoglobin
15.2 g/dL

45.4%

9700/mcL

Serum chemistry profile: Normal
ECG: Sinus rhythm; no signs of arrhythmia or ischemia

The patient’s family has now arrived at the hospital. They state that:
Medical history: Osteoarthritis; intermittent, well-controlled asthma; no recent hospitalizations
Surgical history: Tonsillectomy during childhood
Medications: Albuterol inhaler as needed, OTC fish oil capsules, aspirin as needed
Allergies: No known drug allergies
Family history: Noncontributory
Social history: Social drinker; no other recreational drug use, never smoked cigarettes or used

Repeat temperature is 37° C. Repeat neurologic exam shows normal gait, balance, and motor

Dilated right lateral ventricle

Mild cerebral edema

Vignette:
A 16-year-old male competitive swimmer presents with a 4-day history of progressive right ear pain and itching. He has been swimming daily for the past 3 weeks during summer training. The pain worsens when he chews food and when he lies on his right side. He reports a sensation of fullness in the ear and mild hearing reduction. He denies fever, ear discharge, or recent upper respiratory symptoms. On examination, vital signs are normal. There is marked tenderness on manipulation of the right tragus and with traction on the right auricle. Otoscopic examination reveals a narrowed, edematous external auditory canal with erythematous, macerated skin and scant white debris. The tympanic membrane is barely visible but appears intact. The left ear examination is normal. There is no periauricular lymphadenopathy, mastoid tenderness, or facial nerve dysfunction.

Vignette:
A 35-year-old female office worker presents with a dull, bilateral headache described as a band-like pressure around her head. The headache started in the late afternoon after a long day of meetings and computer work. She rates the pain as 4 out of 10. She denies nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, or visual changes. There is no aura. She reports similar headaches occurring a few times per month for the past year. On examination, vital signs are normal. There is mild tenderness of the bilateral temporal and occipital muscles on palpation. Neurological examination is entirely normal. Fundoscopic exam is unremarkable.

Vignette:
A 25-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician after experiencing her fourth episode in the past 6 weeks of sudden-onset palpitations, shortness of breath, chest tightness, diaphoresis, trembling, and an intense fear of dying. The episodes reach peak intensity within minutes and typically last 15 to 30 minutes before gradually subsiding. Between episodes she has developed significant anticipatory anxiety and has begun avoiding crowded places such as shopping malls and public transportation. She has presented to the emergency department twice during episodes, where cardiac workup including ECG, troponin, and chest radiograph were normal. She has no medical history and no family history of cardiac disease. Vital signs today are normal. Physical examination is unremarkable. Thyroid function tests, CBC, and basic metabolic panel are normal. A 24-hour Holter monitor showed sinus tachycardia during one symptomatic episode only.

Vignette:
A 30-year-old man presents with 2 days of loose watery stools, occurring 3 to 4 times per day, since returning from a vacation in Mexico. He denies blood or mucus in the stool, fever, or vomiting. He reports mild abdominal cramping that is intermittent and not severe. He is maintaining adequate oral hydration. He has no significant past medical history. On examination, vital signs are normal. The abdomen is soft, non-tender, with active bowel sounds. There are no signs of dehydration. He appears well and is in no distress.

Vignette:
A 12-year-old boy is brought in by his mother after experiencing a brief nosebleed from his left nostril approximately 30 minutes ago. The bleeding lasted about 5 minutes and stopped with firm pinching of the nose. His mother reports the house has been very dry due to winter heating, and she has noticed him picking his nose frequently. He denies any history of easy bruising, prolonged bleeding from cuts, or prior nosebleeds requiring medical attention. On examination, there is a small dried blood clot visible at the anterior septum of the left nostril. No active bleeding is noted. The remainder of the nasal exam is normal.

Vignette:
A 38-year-old man with no significant history of back pain developed acute LBP when lifting boxes 2 weeks ago. The pain is aching in nature, located in the left lumbar area, and associated with spasms. He describes previous similar episodes several years ago, which resolved without seeing a doctor. He denies any leg pain or weakness. He also denies fevers, chills, weight loss, and recent infections. Over-the-counter ibuprofen has helped somewhat, but he has taken it only twice a day for the past 3 days because he does not want to become dependent on painkillers. On examination, there is decreased lumbar flexion and extension secondary to pain, but a neurologic exam is unremarkable.

Vignette:
A 45-year-old man presents with the complaint that he has not had a bowel movement in 5 days. He works a sedentary office job and admits to a diet low in fruits, vegetables, and fiber. He drinks approximately 3 cups of coffee daily but only 2-3 glasses of water. He denies abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, blood in stool, or unintentional weight loss. He has no prior surgical history. On examination, the abdomen is soft, non-distended, with mild fullness palpable in the left lower quadrant. Bowel sounds are present and normal.

Vignette:
A 6-year-old boy with a medical history significant for mild persistent asthma is brought to the clinic by his mother with a history of a 5-day cough. His mother reports that the child's fever continues to be elevated despite acetaminophen therapy. He has missed school for the past 3 days and he has a classmate sick with pneumonia. The mother reports that the appetite is good for the child. His cough produced yellowish sputum at home. His vitals at the clinic are: respiratory rate 19 breaths/min, heart rate 80 beats/min, and temperature 101.6°F (38.7°C). He appears in no respiratory distress. His lung examination reveals bilateral rales and occasional wheeze. CXR reveals lobar infiltrates without pleural effusions.

Vignette:
A 30-year-old woman, 10 days postpartum after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery, presents with sudden-onset right-sided pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath that began 2 hours ago while breastfeeding. She reports mild right calf swelling for the past 3 days that she attributed to normal postpartum changes. On examination, she is tachypneic and anxious. Vital signs: T 37.3C, HR 118, RR 26, BP 98/62, SpO2 91% on room air. Right calf is 3 cm larger in circumference than the left with a palpable cord. Lungs are clear. D-dimer is elevated at 4,200 ng/mL. CT pulmonary angiography reveals bilateral segmental and subsegmental pulmonary emboli with right heart strain.

Vignette:
A 22-year-old man is brought in by EMS after a high-speed motorcycle collision 15 minutes ago. He was wearing a helmet but was thrown from the bike and struck a guardrail on the right side. On arrival, he is in severe respiratory distress, gasping for air, and unable to speak in full sentences. Vital signs: T 36.4C, HR 138, RR 36, BP 74/48, SpO2 78% on 15L non-rebreather mask. Neck veins are distended and the trachea is deviated to the left. Right hemithorax is hyperresonant to percussion with absent breath sounds. Left lung has normal breath sounds. Subcutaneous emphysema is palpable along the right chest wall and neck. Needle decompression is performed at the right 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line, with an immediate rush of air.

Vignette:
A 48-year-old overweight male mail carrier with a BMI of 31 presents with a 2-month history of sharp stabbing pain in the bottom of his right heel. The pain is most severe with the first few steps in the morning and after standing up from prolonged sitting, then gradually improves with activity but returns after extended periods of walking on his mail route. He walks approximately 8 miles daily on pavement. He wears standard-issue work boots without orthotic inserts. He denies any trauma, numbness, tingling, or night pain. On examination, there is exquisite point tenderness over the medial calcaneal tubercle at the origin of the plantar fascia. Pain is reproduced with passive dorsiflexion of the toes (windlass test). Achilles tendon is nontender and intact. Heel fat pad is unremarkable. There is tightness of the gastrocnemius-soleus complex bilaterally. Neurovascular examination is intact. Weight-bearing lateral foot radiograph shows a small calcaneal spur, which is noted to be an incidental and common finding.

Vignette:
A 4-year-old boy presents with a 7-day history of abdominal pain and watery diarrhea that became bloody after the first day. Three days before the onset of symptoms, he had visited the county fair with his family and had eaten a hamburger. Physical examination reveals a mild anemia

Vignette:

Vignette:

She reports her hair has become thin and brittle and she has noticed puffiness around her eyes in the morning. Her menstrual periods have become heavier and more irregular. There is periorbital edema and non-pitting edema of the lower extremities. The thyroid gland is diffusely enlarged without nodules. Deep tendon reflexes show delayed relaxation phase. TSH is markedly elevated at 48 mIU/L and free T4 is low at 0.4 ng/dL. Anti-TPO antibodies are positive.

Vignette:
A 48-year-old woman with a history of migraine headaches presents to the emergency room with altered mental status over the last several hours. Preliminary laboratory studies are notable for a serum ALT of 6498 units/L, total bilirubin of 5.6 mg/dL, and INR of 6.8. Her husband reports that she has consistently been taking pain medications and started taking additional 500 mg acetaminophen pills several days ago for lower back pain. Further history reveals a medication list with multiple acetaminophen-containing preparations.

Vignette:
A 68-year-old woman who has followed a strict vegan diet for the past 12 years presents with a 4-month history of progressive tingling and numbness in both feet, fatigue, and difficulty with balance. She reports her tongue has been sore intermittently. She has noticed increased forgetfulness and mild cognitive slowing. She takes no supplements. On examination, vital signs are normal. She appears pale with a smooth, beefy red tongue (glossitis). Neurological examination reveals diminished vibration and proprioception in both feet and ankles, absent ankle reflexes, and a positive Romberg sign. Gait is wide-based and mildly ataxic. Upper extremity neurological exam is normal. CBC reveals hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL with an MCV of 112 fL. Peripheral blood smear shows macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils. Serum B12 level is critically low at 85 pg/mL (normal 200-900). Methylmalonic acid and homocysteine levels are both elevated.

Vignette:
A 42-year-old woman presents with 8 hours of severe, constant epigastric pain radiating straight through to the back, rated 9/10. The pain began after a fatty meal and is associated with persistent nausea and multiple episodes of vomiting. She has a history of cholelithiasis diagnosed 6 months ago but declined elective cholecystectomy. On examination, she is lying very still with her knees drawn up. Vital signs: T 38.2C, HR 116, RR 22, BP 96/58, SpO2 96%. Abdomen is tender in the epigastrium with guarding but no rebound. Bowel sounds are diminished. Labs: lipase 2,840 U/L (normal <60), WBC 16,200/mcL, AST 210 U/L, ALT 185 U/L, total bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL, calcium 7.8 mg/dL. CT abdomen with contrast demonstrates a diffusely edematous pancreas with peripancreatic fluid collections and no evidence of necrosis. BISAP score is 3.

Vignette:
An 18-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents with 4 days of profuse watery diarrhea (10-12 episodes daily) and vomiting (6-8 episodes daily). They report he has been increasingly listless and has had no wet diapers in the past 10 hours. He recently started daycare and several children there have been ill with gastroenteritis. On examination, the infant is limp and lethargic with a weak, barely audible cry. Vital signs: T 38.2C, HR 182, RR 32, BP 68/38 (hypotensive for age), capillary refill 5 seconds. The anterior fontanelle is markedly sunken. Eyes appear deeply sunken with absent tears. Mucous membranes are parched. Skin tenting persists for more than 3 seconds when pinched. Weight is 9.8 kg (previous weight at well-child visit 2 weeks ago was 11.2 kg, representing a 12.5% weight loss). Labs: sodium 158 mEq/L, potassium 2.8 mEq/L, BUN 42 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL (elevated for age), bicarbonate 12 mEq/L, glucose 62 mg/dL. IV normal saline bolus 20 mL/kg is initiated.

Vignette:
A 40-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with a 2-month history of intermittent upper abdominal pain. He describes the pain as a dull, gnawing ache. The pain sometimes wakes him at night, is relieved by food and drinking milk, and is helped partially by ranitidine. He had a similar but milder episode about 5 years ago, which was treated with omeprazole. Physical examination reveals a fit, apparently healthy man in no distress. The only abnormal finding is mild epigastric tenderness on palpation of the abdomen.

Vignette:
An 18-year-old man presents with dry, cracked lips that have persisted for the past 2 weeks. He reports the condition worsened with the onset of cold, dry winter weather. He admits to habitual lip-licking throughout the day. He denies any angular fissures, oral lesions, recent new lip products, or medications such as isotretinoin. He has no history of atopic dermatitis. On examination, the vermilion border of both lips is dry with fine vertical fissures and mild peeling. There is no bleeding, crusting, or angular cheilitis. The perioral skin is mildly dry but not erythematous. The oral mucosa is normal.

Vignette:
An 8-year-old boy in Oklahoma is brought to the emergency department over the fourth of July weekend because of fever, chills, malaise, athralgias, and a headache. Physical examination reveals a maculopapular rash that is most prominent on his wrists and ankles.

Vignette:
A 22-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of bloating, excessive gas, and loose stools that occur approximately 30 minutes after consuming dairy products. She first noticed the pattern about 6 months ago. She denies symptoms when avoiding dairy. She has no abdominal pain between episodes, no blood in stool, no weight loss, and no fever. She has no family history of inflammatory bowel disease or celiac disease. On examination, the abdomen is soft, mildly distended with tympany to percussion, and non-tender. Bowel sounds are active. No masses or organomegaly are noted.

Vignette:

Vignette:
A 17-year-old male student presents with recurrent mouth ulceration since his early schooldays. He has no respiratory, anogenital, gastrointestinal, eye, or skin lesions. His mother had a similar history as a teenager. The social history includes no tobacco use and virtually no alcohol consumption. He has no history of recent drug or medication ingestion. Extraoral exam reveals no significant abnormalities and specifically no pyrexia

Vignette:
A 42-year-old man with a history of Crohn disease managed with azathioprine presents with a 3-day history of burning pain along the left side of his chest followed by the eruption of grouped vesicles on an erythematous base. The rash follows a band-like distribution along the T5 dermatome and does not cross the midline. He reports associated malaise and low-grade fever. Vital signs are stable with temperature 99.8°F. On examination, there are clustered vesicles in various stages, some with clear fluid and others beginning to crust. There is notable allodynia in the affected dermatome. No ocular or facial involvement is present.

Vignette:
A 12-year-old girl presents with sudden-onset severe generalized abdominal pain associated with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. On exam she appears ill and has a temperature of 104°F (40°C). Her abdomen is tense with generalized tenderness and guarding. No bowel sounds are present.

Vignette:
A 30-year-old man presents with a painful, swollen right eye for the past day. He reports minor pain on palpation of the eyelid and denies any history of trauma, crusting, or change in vision. He has no history of allergies or any eye conditions and denies the use of any new soaps, lotions, or creams. On exam, he has localized tenderness to palpation and erythema on the midline of the lower eyelid near the lid margin. The remainder of the physical exam, including the globe, is normal.

Vignette:
A 78-year-old man is brought in after a syncopal episode at home witnessed by his wife. She reports he has been increasingly fatigued and lightheaded for the past week. His past medical history includes aortic stenosis, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes. On examination, he is alert but pale and mildly confused. Vital signs: T 36.6C, HR 32, RR 18, BP 82/50, SpO2 93%. Cannon A waves are visible in the jugular venous pulse. Heart sounds reveal a systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border and variable intensity of S1. ECG demonstrates complete atrioventricular dissociation with a ventricular escape rate of 32 bpm, wide QRS complexes, and independent P waves at a rate of 82 bpm.

Vignette:
A 28-year-old man presents to his physician with a 5-day history of fever, chills, and rigors, not improving with acetaminophen (paracetamol), along with diarrhea. He had been traveling in Central America for 3 months, returning 8 weeks ago. He had been bitten by mosquitoes on multiple occasions, and although he initially took malaria prophylaxis, he discontinued it due to mild nausea. He does not know the specifics of his prophylactic therapy. On examination he has a temperature of 100.4°F (38°C), and is mildly tachycardic with a BP of 126/82 mmHg. The remainder of the examination is normal.

Vignette:
A 56-year-old man presents to urgent care with acute onset of excruciating pain in his right great toe that woke him from sleep at 3 AM. The pain developed rapidly over several hours and is now the worst pain he has ever experienced, rated 10 out of 10. He reports the toe is so sensitive that even the weight of a bedsheet is unbearable. He had a steak dinner with several beers the evening before onset. His past medical history includes hypertension managed with hydrochlorothiazide and hyperlipidemia. He is overweight with a BMI of 30. On examination, the right first metatarsophalangeal joint is intensely erythematous, swollen, warm, and exquisitely tender to even light palpation. Active and passive range of motion is severely limited by pain. Vital signs show temperature 99.4°F, heart rate 88. Serum uric acid is 9.8 mg/dL. Inflammatory markers show ESR 42 and CRP 6.2.

Vignette:
A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes managed with glipizide and metformin is found confused and diaphoretic on his living room floor by his daughter. She reports he has had poor oral intake for the past 2 days due to a gastrointestinal illness with vomiting and diarrhea but continued taking all medications. On examination by EMS, he is obtunded, drenched in sweat, and exhibiting intermittent tremors. Vital signs: T 35.8C, HR 108, RR 20, BP 162/94, SpO2 96%. Finger-stick glucose reads 28 mg/dL. Neurological exam shows bilateral extensor plantar responses, generalized hyperreflexia, and no focal deficits. EMS administers 25 g of dextrose 50% IV with improvement in mental status within minutes, but glucose subsequently drops again to 42 mg/dL, requiring a continuous dextrose 10% infusion.

Vignette:
A 34-year-old male with a history of HIV (CD4 count 45 cells/mcL, not on antiretroviral therapy) presents with a 2-week history of progressive dyspnea, dry cough, and low-grade fevers. He reports significant fatigue and an unintentional 10-pound weight loss over the past month. On examination, he appears cachectic and is in mild respiratory distress. Vital signs: T 38.4C, HR 112, RR 28, BP 108/68, SpO2 88% on room air. Lung auscultation reveals bilateral diffuse crackles. Chest X-ray shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates with a ground-glass pattern. LDH is markedly elevated at 580 U/L. Induced sputum is sent for silver stain.

Vignette:
A 7-month-old girl is brought in by her parents who report she has been unusually fussy for the past 3 days. They have noticed increased drooling and that she constantly chews on her fingers and toys. She is eating slightly less than usual but still taking adequate formula. She has no fever, no diarrhea, and no rash. On examination, temperature is 37.0°C. The infant is mildly irritable but consolable. The lower gingiva is mildly swollen and erythematous over the area of the central incisors, and a tooth bud is palpable beneath the surface. The remainder of the exam is normal.

Vignette:
A 48-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of recurrent episodes of severe spinning vertigo lasting 2 to 4 hours per episode, occurring approximately twice monthly. Each episode is preceded by a sensation of fullness in her right ear and accompanied by roaring tinnitus and reduced hearing on the right side. Between episodes she notes persistent mild tinnitus and a sense that her right ear hearing has gradually deteriorated. She experiences nausea and sometimes vomiting during attacks. She denies headache, visual changes, or focal neurological symptoms. Audiometry demonstrates low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss in the right ear with normal hearing on the left. On examination between episodes, vital signs are normal. The Rinne test shows air conduction greater than bone conduction bilaterally. Weber test lateralizes to the left ear. Neurological exam is nonfocal.

Vignette:
Mr. E is a 26 year-old man who presents to your office for complaints of sore throat, headache, and non-productive cough. His symptoms started 2 days ago with acute onset of sore throat. He has been afebrile. His physical examination is normal, except for some pharyngeal erythema. He is otherwise in good health, and is on no medications except for acetaminophen for his sore throat and fever. He has no drug allergies.

Vignette:
Mr. Y is a 64 year old Chinese male who presents with chest pain for 24 hours. One day prior to presentation, the patient began to experience 8/10, non-radiating substernal chest pressure associated with diaphoresis and shortness of breath. The pain intially improved with Tylenol, however over the following 24 hours, his symptoms worsened. The patient went to his primary physician, where an EKG was performed which showed ST elevation in leads V2-V6.

Vignette:
A 15-year-old girl presents with a superficial scrape on her left knee after falling off her skateboard approximately 1 hour ago. She was wearing shorts and fell onto pavement. On examination, there is a 6 by 4 cm superficial abrasion on the anterior left knee with minor oozing of serous fluid. Vignette:
A 65-year-old man with hypertension and degenerative joint disease presents to the emergency department with a three-day history of a productive cough and fever. A 33-year-old man presents with a several-month history of persistent flaky, scaly patches on his scalp and eyebrows. He reports mild itching that is worse after showering. There are no excoriations or signs of secondary infection.

Vignette:
A 3-year-old boy is brought in by his mother after 6 days of persistent high fever unresponsive to acetaminophen and ibuprofen. He has been increasingly irritable and refusing to eat. On examination, the child is febrile, irritable, and difficult to console. Vital signs: T 39.6C, HR 148, RR 28, BP 86/52. Bilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection is present. Lips are erythematous with fissures. A prominent strawberry tongue is noted. A diffuse polymorphous maculopapular rash covers the trunk and perineum with early desquamation in the groin. Bilateral hands and feet show indurative edema with erythema. Right anterior cervical lymphadenopathy measuring 2.0 cm is palpable. Labs: WBC 18,600/mcL, ESR 82 mm/hr, CRP 12.4 mg/dL, albumin 2.6 g/dL, platelets 488,000/mcL, ALT 68 U/L. Echocardiogram reveals dilated left anterior descending coronary artery (z-score 3.2). IVIG and high-dose aspirin are initiated.

On examination, the right wrist has full range of motion. There is mild tenderness along the dorsal extensor tendons without visible swelling or erythema. Finkelstein test is negative. Grip strength is mildly reduced compared to the left. Neurovascular exam is intact.

Today, she says it feels as though air escapes through her nose while speaking, giving it a

diplopia, drooping eyelids, loss of smell or taste, and difficulty with balance or gait. She denies
having arm and leg weakness and numbness.

Skin: Noncontributory

Vignette:

Vignette:
A 28-year-old woman who is 3 weeks postpartum and exclusively breastfeeding presents with a 2-day history of increasing pain, redness, and swelling in her right breast. She reports associated fever and chills and feeling generally unwell. She had been experiencing nipple soreness and cracking on the right side and notes the baby has had difficulty latching on that side. She denies palpable masses or nipple discharge other than breast milk. Vital signs show temperature 101.2°F, heart rate 94, blood pressure 118/72. On examination, there is a wedge-shaped area of erythema, warmth, and induration in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast. The area is exquisitely tender to palpation. There is no fluctuance or palpable abscess. The ipsilateral nipple shows a small fissure. Axillary lymph nodes are mildly enlarged on the right.

Vignette:
A 22-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes diagnosed at age 8 presents with 2 days of worsening nausea, vomiting, diffuse abdominal pain, and progressive lethargy. She reports that she ran out of insulin 3 days ago and could not afford a refill. On examination, she is drowsy but arousable, markedly dehydrated with dry mucous membranes and poor skin turgor. Vignette:
A 58-year-old man presents with sudden onset of severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back between his shoulder blades that began 45 minutes ago while lifting heavy boxes. He has a history of poorly controlled hypertension and takes amlodipine intermittently. On examination, he is writhing in pain and appears ashen. Vital signs: T 36.8C, HR 108, RR 24, BP 210/118 in the right arm and 162/90 in the left arm. A diastolic murmur is auscultated along the left sternal border. Pulses are diminished in the left upper extremity. Chest X-ray shows widened mediastinum. CT angiography of the chest reveals a Stanford type A dissection originating in the ascending aorta with an intimal flap extending into the aortic arch.

Vignette:
A 65-year-old man with a history of metastatic prostate cancer (Gleason 9, diagnosed 2 years ago) presents with 10 days of progressive mid-back pain and 4 days of increasing difficulty walking. He now requires a walker. He also reports a band-like sensation around his trunk at the level of the umbilicus and difficulty initiating urination. On examination, he appears cachectic. Vital signs are stable. Neurological exam reveals increased tone and spasticity in both lower extremities, bilateral lower extremity weakness (3/5 hip flexors, 4/5 knee extensors), hyperreflexia with bilateral ankle clonus, upgoing plantar responses (positive Babinski bilaterally), and a sensory level at approximately T10. MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrates a large epidural mass at T9-T10 causing significant spinal cord compression with cord signal changes.

Vignette:
A 28-year-old man presents with a persistent dry cough for the past 10 days. He reports that the cough started after a mild upper respiratory illness with sore throat and nasal congestion that has since resolved. He is a non-smoker and has no history of asthma or chronic lung disease. He denies fever, hemoptysis, or significant sputum production. On examination, vital signs are within normal limits. Lungs reveal occasional scattered rhonchi that clear with coughing. There are no wheezes or crackles. Oxygen saturation is 98% on room air.

Vignette:
A 22-year-old sexually active man presents with a 4-day history of gradually worsening left scrotal pain and swelling. The pain is dull and aching and radiates to the left inguinal region. He reports mild dysuria and a small amount of urethral discharge noticed over the past week. He has had a new sexual partner in the past month and inconsistently uses barrier protection. He denies fever, nausea, vomiting, or testicular trauma. Vital signs are normal. On examination, the left hemiscrotum is swollen and erythematous. There is tenderness and induration localized to the left epididymis posterior to the testis. Prehn sign is positive with relief of pain on elevation of the left testis. The cremasteric reflex is present bilaterally. There is no testicular torsion on clinical assessment. Urinalysis shows 15 to 20 WBC per high-power field. A nucleic acid amplification test for chlamydia and gonorrhea is sent.

Vignette:
An 18-month-old toddler presents with 1 week of rhinorrhea, cough, and congestion. Her parents report she is irritable, sleeping restlessly, and not eating well. Overnight she developed a fever. She attends day care and both parents smoke. On examination signs are found consistent with a viral respiratory infection including rhinorrhea and congestion. The toddler appears irritable and apprehensive and has a fever. Otoscopy reveals a bulging, erythematous tympanic membrane and absent landmarks.

Vignette:
A 30-year-old man presents with a painful fluid-filled blister on his right heel that developed after a 15-kilometer hike in recently purchased boots yesterday. He reports the boots felt slightly tight in the heel area. He denies any popping of the blister or signs of infection. He has no history of diabetes or peripheral neuropathy. On examination, there is a single, tense, clear fluid-filled blister approximately 2 cm in diameter on the posterior right heel. The surrounding skin is mildly erythematous. There is no purulence, surrounding warmth, streaking, or malodor. Pedal pulses are intact and sensation is normal.

Vignette:
A 42-year-old female data entry clerk presents with a 4-month history of numbness, tingling, and burning sensation in her right thumb, index finger, middle finger, and radial half of the ring finger. Symptoms are worse at night and frequently wake her from sleep. She reports shaking her hand provides temporary relief. She has also noticed progressive weakness in her grip, with difficulty holding small objects and occasional dropping of items. She works 8 hours daily at a keyboard with minimal ergonomic support. She has a history of well-controlled hypothyroidism. On examination, there is decreased sensation to two-point discrimination in the median nerve distribution. Thenar eminence shows early atrophy compared to the left. Tinel sign at the wrist is positive with paresthesias radiating to the fingers. Phalen test reproduces symptoms within 20 seconds. Grip and pinch strength are reduced on the right.

A 12-year-old boy is brought by his parents for a persistent cough that has lasted 3 weeks and is progressively worsening. She had been recuperating at home but on beginning to mobilize and walk, the right leg became painful, tender, and swollen. On examination, the right calf is 4 cm greater in circumference than the left when measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity. Vignette:
A 60-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of a painful, burning, vesicular rash on the left side of her forehead extending to the tip of her nose. She initially experienced a prodrome of tingling and deep aching pain over the left forehead for 2 days before the rash appeared. She now reports left eye redness, tearing, photophobia, and a gritty foreign body sensation. She has a history of well-controlled hypertension and had chickenpox as a child. She has not received the herpes zoster vaccine. On examination, temperature is 99.4°F. There are grouped vesicles on an erythematous base distributed along the left V1 (ophthalmic) division of the trigeminal nerve, involving the forehead, upper eyelid, and the tip of the nose (positive Hutchinson sign). The left eye shows conjunctival injection, mild periorbital edema, and a mildly hazy cornea. Visual acuity is 20/40 on the left (baseline 20/25) and 20/25 on the right. Intraocular pressure is 14 mmHg bilaterally. The right side of the face is entirely clear.

Vignette:
A 3-week-old male neonate is brought in by his mother who reports that the baby has been feeding poorly for the past 12 hours and seems unusually sleepy. Vignette:
A 45-year-old man is brought in by EMS after sustaining a stab wound to the left anterior chest approximately 20 minutes ago. He is conscious but confused and increasingly agitated. On examination, there is a 3 cm wound at the 5th intercostal space, left parasternal line, with minimal external bleeding. Vital signs: T 36.5C, HR 132, RR 28, BP 78/64, SpO2 94%. Neck veins are markedly distended. Heart sounds are muffled and distant. Lungs are clear bilaterally. He has pulsus paradoxus with a 22 mmHg drop in systolic pressure during inspiration. Bedside FAST ultrasound reveals a large pericardial effusion with right ventricular diastolic collapse consistent with tamponade physiology.

Vignette:
A 63-year-old man sustained a cut on his hand while gardening. His immunization history is significant for not having received a complete tetanus immunization schedule. He presents with signs of generalized tetanus with trismus ("lock jaw"), which results in a grimace described as "risus sardonicus" (sardonic smile). Intermittent tonic contraction of his skeletal muscles causes intensely painful spasms, which last for minutes, during which he retains consciousness. The spasms are triggered by external (noise, light, drafts, physical contact) or internal stimuli, and as a result he is at the risk of sustaining fractures or developing rhabdomyolysis. The tetanic spasms also produce opisthotonus, board-like abdominal wall rigidity, dysphagia, and apneic periods due to contraction of the thoracic muscles and/or glottal or pharyngeal muscles. During a generalized spasm the patient arches his back, extends his legs, flexes his arms in abduction, and clenches his fists. Apnea results during some of the spasms. Autonomic overactivity initially manifests as irritability, restlessness, sweating, and tachycardia. Several days later this may present as hyperpyrexia, cardiac arrhythmias, labile hypertension, or hypotension.

Vignette:
A 32-year-old woman with a history of Graves disease (non-compliant with methimazole for 2 months) presents with 2 days of palpitations, agitation, profuse sweating, and diarrhea. She had a dental extraction 3 days ago. On examination, she is markedly agitated, tremulous, and unable to remain still. Vital signs: T 40.0C (104F), HR 162 (atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response), RR 28, BP 168/60 (widened pulse pressure), SpO2 97%. She has a fine tremor, bilateral proptosis, lid lag, diffuse goiter with an audible bruit, and brisk reflexes throughout. Skin is warm and moist. She becomes increasingly confused during the examination. Labs: TSH <0.01 mIU/L, free T4 7.8 ng/dL (normal 0.8-1.8), free T3 22 pg/mL (normal 2.3-4.2). Burch-Wartofsky score is 65 (highly suggestive of thyroid storm). Propranolol, PTU, hydrocortisone, and iodine solution are initiated.

Vignette:
A 35-year-old man who is an avid hiker in Connecticut presents with a 5-day history of an expanding red rash on his right thigh that he noticed after a weekend camping trip two weeks ago. He recalls removing an engorged tick from his thigh. He now reports fatigue, mild headache, arthralgias in his knees and wrists, and low-grade fever. He denies neck stiffness, facial weakness, chest pain, or palpitations. On examination, temperature is 99.6°F. There is a 12 cm annular erythematous plaque on the right anterior thigh with central clearing, consistent with erythema migrans. There are no secondary skin lesions. Joints are nontender without effusion. Neurological examination is nonfocal. Heart rate is regular at 74 with no murmurs. There is no cervical rigidity.

Vignette:
A 6-week-old male infant is brought in by his parents who are concerned about episodes of inconsolable crying that occur most evenings. The crying episodes last 2 to 3 hours, during which the baby draws up his knees and appears to be in distress. The episodes typically begin around 6 PM and resolve by bedtime. Between episodes, the infant is calm and content. He is exclusively breastfed, feeding well, and gaining weight along the 50th percentile. He has no fever, vomiting, or bloody stools. On examination, the infant is calm and alert. Abdomen is soft and non-distended with normal bowel sounds. Fontanelles are flat. The exam is entirely normal.

Vignette:

She reports prior exposure to a person who had a runny nose and a hacking cough. She did not receive significant relief from her rescue inhaler with worsening symptoms, despite increased use. She has been compliant with her maintenance asthma regimen, which consists of an inhaled corticosteroid and a leukotriene receptor antagonist for maintenance therapy and albuterol as rescue therapy. Her cough is disrupting her sleep pattern and as a consequence she is experiencing daytime somnolence, which is affecting her job performance.

Vignette:

Vignette:

The scales are thick in some areas. The parents report the baby is feeding well, gaining weight appropriately, and sleeping normally. There is no rash elsewhere on the body. On examination, there are adherent yellowish-white greasy scales over the anterior fontanelle and vertex of the scalp. There is no underlying erythema, no oozing, and no involvement of the face or diaper area. The infant is content and thriving.

Vignette:

Vital signs show temperature 101.8°F, heart rate 96, blood pressure 110/68, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. She has no signs of respiratory distress or dehydration.

Vignette:

On examination, a single shallow oval ulcer approximately 5 mm in diameter is visible on the buccal mucosa of the left cheek. It has a white-yellowish base with an erythematous halo. The remainder of the oral exam is unremarkable. There is no lymphadenopathy.

Vignette:

A dermoscopic examination reveals arborizing vessels and blue-gray ovoid nests.
